title.$t: The Nobel Prize’s Missing Fourth Chair: The Researcher Does the Work, the Lab Head Gets the Medal

content.$t:
On a research paper, the first name belongs to the researcher who did the hard work, and the last to the head of the lab. But the name that reaches the Nobel stage is usually the last one: not the people who made the discovery, but the people who led it.

This article was first published in Nepali on Shilapatra on October 20, 2026 (Kartik 3, 2083 BS). This is the author’s own English translation.

The article’s header as published on Shilapatra.

The Nobel That Didn’t Know Ed Boyden

Monday, October 5, 2026.

As it does every year, the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm announced this year’s Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. This year’s prize went to optogenetics, a technique that uses light to switch the brain’s nerve cells (neurons) on or off at will.

In short

  • A Nobel Prize can be shared by at most three people, and it is not given to anyone who has died.
  • On a research paper, the first name usually belongs to the student or researcher who did the work, and the last to the head of the lab. The Nobel usually goes to the last name.
  • The 2026 medicine prize for optogenetics went to Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel, but not to Ed Boyden, first author of the 2005 paper that launched the field.
  • Shohei Hori, Rosalind Lee, Douglas Prasher, Jocelyn Bell and Albert Schatz were left out the same way.
  • In 1903, Pierre Curie’s letter put Marie Curie on the Nobel stage, a rare exception.

In his will, Alfred Nobel arranged for each prize to be chosen by a separate institution. Every year the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences picks the physics and chemistry prizes, the Karolinska Institutet picks medicine, the Swedish Academy picks literature, and the Norwegian Nobel Committee picks the peace prize. Some of the Nobel rules, though, were made later, and two of them are very strict. A prize can be shared by at most three people, and it cannot be given to someone who has died.

A prize can be shared by at most three people, and it cannot be given to someone who has died.

This time there were three medicine laureates: Karl Deisseroth of the United States, and Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel of Germany. No one disputes the contribution of Hegemann and Nagel, who discovered a protein in green algae that opens in response to light. The question is about the two people who put it to use in nerve cells: the third person the prize recognized, and the fourth who did not fit.

Within hours of the announcement, one question was going around social media: where is Ed Boyden? On the 2005 paper that laid the foundation of optogenetics, the first name was Boyden’s and the last was Deisseroth’s. That paper, which showed how the protein Nagel and Hegemann had discovered could be used in nerve cells, is what started the new field of optogenetics.

At the time, Boyden and Deisseroth were both at Stanford University. Boyden, who was doing his PhD in another lab, worked on optogenetics with Deisseroth as a side project. Deisseroth was just starting his independent career.

Today Deisseroth is a professor at Stanford, and Boyden is at MIT. The optogenetics paper that Boyden began as a side project won the Nobel. The Nobel committee recognized Deisseroth, but there was no fourth chair for Boyden.

Every year, during Nobel week, the story of Boyden and Deisseroth repeats itself. On every research paper, the first name belongs to the student or researcher who played the main role in the work, and the last to the senior researcher or head of the lab. Prizes and credit alike usually recognize the author whose name comes last.

This story is not only this year’s, and it is not new. The history of science is full of Ed Boydens. But there was one scientist who turned this custom upside down 123 years ago.

Marie Curie: The First Woman to Win a Nobel Prize

June 25, 1903, the Sorbonne, Paris.

A thirty-five-year-old Polish woman stood before her examiners to defend her PhD research. The subject of her thesis was “Research on Radioactive Substances”.

Exactly six years earlier, she had started her PhD research by picking up a small question. The French scientist Henri Becquerel had already shown that uranium gives off an invisible “new kind” of ray. But what the ray was, how strong it was, and whether other substances gave it off too, no one knew. She set out to follow it. She found that thorium, not only uranium, gave off the same kind of rays, and she named the phenomenon “radioactivity”.

When she began, it was already known that uranium was radioactive. But no one had noticed that pitchblende, the mineral uranium is mined from, contains another element far more radioactive than uranium. While measuring the radioactivity of pitchblende, that new element caught her attention, and finding out what it was became the heart of her PhD.

By this point her husband had set aside his own research to join her. Within 1898 the two of them found two new elements, polonium and radium. They spent the next four years in a leaky shed, boiling tons of pitchblende and stirring it with an iron rod as tall as themselves, to separate pure radium.

The researcher standing before the examiners on June 25, 1903 was Marie Curie, and sitting in the audience was her husband and colleague, Pierre Curie.

Early in 1903, members of the French Academy of Sciences had nominated two people for that year’s Nobel Prize in Physics: Henri Becquerel and Pierre Curie. The woman whose question and research had started it all did not even make the list.

That year the Swedish mathematician Gösta Mittag-Leffler sat on the Nobel committee. This bothered him, and he wrote to Pierre, telling him that only his name had been put forward for the prize. In August, Pierre wrote back: “If it is true that one is seriously thinking about me for the prize, I very much wish to be considered together with Madame Curie with respect to our research on radioactive bodies.” Many accounts say Pierre declared, “I won’t accept the prize without Marie.” His letter uses no such strong words. It was gentle, but its meaning was clear.

“If it is true that one is seriously thinking about me for the prize, I very much wish to be considered together with Madame Curie.” (Pierre Curie, 1903)

In December 1903, the physics prize was awarded for radioactivity: half to Becquerel and half to the Curies. Marie became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. She is also the only person to win a Nobel for their PhD research. Eight years later, in 1911, she won the chemistry prize alone, for her research on radium and polonium.

Pierre had nothing to lose. His name was already known, the Academy had chosen him, and credit was flowing naturally his way. He simply did not want it to.

But turn the pages of the history of science and you find few people like Pierre. Look no further than the greatest scientist you and I know, Albert Einstein. Two years after Marie’s Nobel Prize, he published five research papers, including E=mc². We know 1905 as Einstein’s miracle year.

His only Nobel Prize (for 1921) was for the work on light he published early that year. His wife Mileva did the mathematics in all those papers. Yet Mileva’s name appears nowhere on any of Einstein’s papers.

The DNA Secret Hidden in a Drawer

Fifty years after Marie’s first Nobel Prize, Linus Pauling in America and James Watson, Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins in Britain were racing to find the structure of DNA. The most important contribution of all came from Rosalind Franklin, but no one valued it at the time.

In early January 1953, Pauling put out a model of DNA, and on January 29 Watson, in Cambridge, got to read it. The next morning Watson went to London to tell Wilkins, “Pauling has proposed a DNA model that doesn’t work either, just like ours.” In Wilkins’s lab at King’s College, empty for the winter break, they spent the whole day discussing what to do next.

Rosalind’s lab was right next to Wilkins’s. Suddenly he remembered a photograph of DNA that Rosalind had taken about eight months earlier. Rosalind was not in the lab that day. He neither asked her permission nor told her, once she was back, that he had shown the photo to Watson. On January 30, 1953, Watson saw Photo 51, which Rosalind and her student Raymond Gosling had taken with an exposure of about 60 hours. It was Photo 51 that revealed the secret of how DNA is built.

Having seen Photo 51, Watson hurried back to Cambridge. On the cold train from London, he sketched the photo’s “X” from memory in the margin of a newspaper. The moment he saw the photo, it was clear to him: DNA is made of two strands in a helix, a double helix. Rosalind’s photo could tell you everything, the length of the helix and the distance between two nucleotides.

For Watson and Crick, Rosalind’s Photo 51 was the eureka moment. Watson later wrote, “The instant I saw the picture my mouth fell open and my pulse began to race.”

Two days after returning from London, they went back to work on DNA. Watson and Crick’s paper on the structure of DNA appeared in Nature on April 25, 1953. Rosalind and Gosling’s paper with Photo 51 was printed in the same issue. The credit for discovering the structure of DNA, and about a decade later the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins.

Rosalind, who took Photo 51, had already died in 1958, at the age of 37. She left King’s College in 1953 on the condition that she would not work on DNA again, and spent the rest of her life researching viruses. The Nobel Prize is still not given to scientists who have died. Even had she lived, she would hardly have fit among the three laureates.

Whose Work, Whose Name?

I have told Rosalind’s story many times. But every time I told it, I repeated the same mistake. With Rosalind at the center of the story, I rarely remembered her PhD student, Raymond Gosling, who worked right beside her. The two of them contributed equally to telling apart the “A” and “B” forms of DNA for the first time.

On May 2, 1952, Rosalind and Gosling took Photo 51 together, an exposure of nearly 60 hours. I remembered the injustice done to Rosalind, but it turns out that I, too, kept forgetting the student who sat beside the camera.

I remembered the injustice done to Rosalind, but it turns out that I, too, kept forgetting the student who sat beside the camera.

But the Rosalind story doesn’t end here. This is not the only time a Rosalind missed a Nobel Prize she deserved.

In 2024, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun for discovering a new kind of RNA called microRNA. The Nobel Prize’s official Twitter account wrote that Ambros celebrated the news with his colleague and wife, Rosalind Lee.

Rosalind was the lead author of the 1993 research paper on microRNA, and the last name on it was Ambros’s. The prize forgot Rosalind and recognized only Ambros.

The same thing happened last year, when the 2025 medicine prize was awarded. Mary Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi won the Nobel for their discoveries about the regulatory cells of our immune system, regulatory T cells (Tregs).

The researcher in Sakaguchi’s lab who showed that the Foxp3 gene controls how Tregs develop and work was Shohei Hori. On the 2003 paper on Tregs and Foxp3, the first name was his and the last was Sakaguchi’s. He did not fit in the prize’s three chairs; the prize recognized only the head of the lab.

Still, last year’s prize also hides a story that runs the other way. Mary Brunkow, who identified the Foxp3 gene in mice in 2001, did win the Nobel. She was not a university professor but a researcher working at a company. Nobel laureates from outside universities are rare.

I myself do research in a university lab in New York. In our world, the first name on a paper usually belongs to the student or postdoc who repeated the experiments for months and produced the data. The last name belongs to the head of the lab (the PI), who set the direction of the research and raised the money. They are also the ones who correspond with the journal when the paper is published. And when prizes are announced or history is written, it is usually their name the world remembers.

Back in 1968, the sociologist Robert Merton called this the “Matthew effect”: whoever is already known gets the credit too. Because it falls even harder on women, the historian Margaret Rossiter named that version the “Matilda effect” in 1993. Leaf through history and the stories of Boyden, Rosalind and Gosling may stop looking like exceptions.

The sociologist Robert Merton called it the “Matthew effect”: whoever is already known gets the credit too.

The Professor Gets the Name, the Researcher Stays Nameless

There was a time when catching tuberculosis (TB) meant waiting to die. The first drug to lift that fear was streptomycin. In 1943, a professor at Rutgers University in the United States kept a 23-year-old student who worked with TB bacteria in the basement of the building, away from everyone else.

The professor never set foot in that lab himself. The student worked there day and night, sometimes sleeping there too. Within a few months, from a bacterium taken from a chicken’s throat, he isolated streptomycin, which could kill the TB bacterium.

The professor’s name was Selman Waksman, and the student was Albert Schatz. On their 1944 paper, the first name was the student’s, and both their names were on the patent. The professor had the student sign his royalties over to the university for one dollar, while he himself quietly kept taking 20 percent of the royalties. When the student found out, he sued in 1950, and in an out-of-court settlement he was recognized as “co-discoverer”.

After he sued his own professor, American universities hesitated to hire him. Two years later, in 1952, Waksman alone received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of streptomycin. Rutgers finally recognized Schatz nearly 50 years later, honoring him in 1994.

Jocelyn Bell and the Signal from Dead Stars

Physics has a similar example of a hardworking student who got no credit. By 1967, on a field outside Cambridge, a radio telescope had been built over two years by stringing thousands of wires across hundreds of posts.

Every day the telescope recorded the signals coming from the sky as lines traced on long rolls of paper. The job of reading those lines and working out what the signals were fell to 24-year-old Jocelyn Bell.

One day in August she noticed a rough, scruffy-looking mark on the paper, about a centimeter long. Someone else might have dismissed it as a glitch in the machine. She remembered it, waited for the same patch of sky again, and found it again. Recorded up close, the signal turned out to be pulsing like a clock, exactly 1.33 seconds apart. No one could believe anything in nature was that regular, so as a joke it was named “LGM-1”, for Little Green Men. Later it turned out to be a dead star spinning extremely fast: a pulsar.

On the paper published in Nature in 1968, the first name was her supervisor Antony Hewish’s, and hers was second. In 1974 the Nobel Prize in Physics went to Hewish and Martin Ryle. Jocelyn herself never complained; she said that giving a Nobel to a student would be right only in exceptional cases.

Jocelyn’s contribution was recognized only later, and she used the prize she received in the same spirit. In 2018 she gave away the whole of the roughly three million dollars of her Breakthrough Prize to students from underrepresented communities who want to study physics.

Lise Meitner and the Atom Worked Out in the Snow

Another physicist who did not complain was Lise Meitner. Before the Second World War, she and her colleague Otto Hahn were already working on what would become nuclear fission. Lise was a woman, and she was Jewish. After nearly thirty years working with Hahn in Berlin, she fled Nazi Germany in July 1938 to save her life and reached Sweden.

Even after she reached Sweden, her work with Hahn went on by letter. In Berlin, when Hahn and his assistant Fritz Strassmann bombarded uranium with neutrons, they found barium, another element about half as heavy as uranium. In December 1938, Hahn wrote to Lise asking her to explain it.

That Christmas holiday, walking in the Swedish snow with her nephew, the physicist Otto Frisch, Lise sat down on a tree trunk and did the calculation. The uranium nucleus had split in two, and the energy released could be measured with Einstein’s own E=mc². Frisch named it “fission”. But Lise’s name was not on Hahn and Strassmann’s paper, published in January 1939. Putting her name on it would have told the Nazis that she was still working with them.

Hahn alone received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; even Strassmann’s name did not come up. Lise was nominated for the Nobel nearly fifty times, but she never won. Why she was left out we learned only much later. When the Nobel files, kept secret for 50 years, were opened in the 1990s, historians wrote that the committee had simply failed to understand Lise’s contribution, which sat on the border between physics and chemistry.

Lise’s name is not on the list of Nobel laureates, but it is on the list of elements: element number 109, meitnerium.

The Glowing Green Gene Sent by Mail

For people like me who work on the immune system, the protein that makes cells glow green (GFP) is an everyday tool. It comes from a species of jellyfish, and the first person to isolate its gene, in 1992, was Douglas Prasher. Right then his research funding ran out. Before leaving science, he mailed the gene, free of charge, to two scientists: Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien.

In 2008, when Osamu Shimomura, who discovered the protein, and Chalfie and Tsien, who researched the gene, won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, Prasher was driving a shuttle van for a car dealership in Alabama. Chalfie and Tsien, though, did not forget him: they invited him to Stockholm at their own expense. When the prize was handed over, Prasher was there too, not on the stage, but in the audience.

When the prize was handed over, Prasher was there too, not on the stage, but in the audience.

The List Doesn’t End Here

Start counting such names and the list never ends. But a few more must be remembered.

In 1921, the team in Canada that discovered insulin included a 22-year-old student, Charles Best. But two years later the Nobel went to Frederick Banting and the head of the lab, John Macleod. Furious that the prize went to Macleod instead of Best, Banting left the lab and gave half of his prize to Best.

Another example is Candace Pert: although she discovered the opiate receptor in the brain during her PhD research, the prize went to three men, including her professor.

Like history itself, science has been most unjust to women. It was Nettie Stevens who showed that the X and Y chromosomes decide whether an animal is male or female, yet for decades textbooks put Edmund B. Wilson’s name first. Marthe Gautier was the first to see the cause of Down syndrome under the microscope, but the world recognized her colleague Jérôme Lejeune.

Some die before any prize can reach them. Alice Ball, who made the first effective injectable treatment for leprosy, died at just 24, and her method went around under the name of her college’s president, as the “Dean method”. Henrietta Leavitt, who found the rule for measuring distances across the universe, had also died before anyone tried to nominate her for the Nobel.

And in our own neighborhood: Satyendra Nath Bose, who sent his mathematics from Dhaka to Einstein, gave his name to a whole family of particles, the “bosons”. Many people later won Nobel Prizes for discoveries about bosons. Bose himself never did.

One Stage, Three Chairs

The Nobel has its own arithmetic: one stage, at most three chairs, and the condition that you must be alive.

The fourth chair: people who did the work but were left off the Nobel stage (created with Claude).

The three-chair rule was made in an era when science was done by one or two people working together. Today a single research paper carries dozens, sometimes hundreds of names, but there are still only three chairs on the Nobel stage. This year there was no fourth chair for Ed Boyden, and in 2008 there was none for Douglas Prasher.

The must-be-alive condition kept Rosalind Franklin, Lise and Henrietta Leavitt out forever. But just how strange this condition is became clear in 2011. That year, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was announced for Ralph Steinman, who discovered the dendritic cells of our immune system. The committee had no idea, but he had died three days earlier. The Nobel Foundation let the prize stand in his name. In other words, who gets a Nobel is sometimes decided not by their contribution but by when the news of a death reaches Stockholm.

But the biggest gap is not in any written rule; it is in science’s unwritten custom. Albert Schatz, Candace Pert, Rosalind Lee, Shohei Hori and Ed Boyden were all the first name on the papers reporting their discoveries. The prize went to the last name, the corresponding author. The corresponding author is the person who corresponds with the journal’s editor and takes responsibility for the paper; it is not proof of who made the discovery. But over time, grants, prizes and history all came to treat that address as the discoverer.

The biggest gap is not in any written rule; it is in science’s unwritten custom.

Not every lab head is a credit thief. Sakaguchi and Deisseroth built their fields through decades of hard work. But the system has become such that no one needs to steal the credit; it flows on its own, looking for whoever sits on top.

A century and a quarter ago, one letter from Pierre Curie refused this custom. Since him, few have written such a letter. In 1923 Banting split his prize money with Best, and in 2008 Chalfie and Tsien brought Prasher to Stockholm. But those remained exceptions.

Early next October, the names of the new Nobel laureates will once again be announced from Stockholm. That day, after you read the winners’ names, open their research papers and look at whose name comes first. Perhaps you will find a Boyden there, a Hori, a Rosalind.

The Nobel doesn’t read their names. Let us, at least.

Frequently asked questions

How many people can share a Nobel Prize?

At most three. The prize also cannot be given to someone who has died, though a laureate who dies after the announcement keeps it. In 2011 the Nobel Foundation let Ralph Steinman’s prize stand, even though he had died three days before the announcement.

Why didn’t Ed Boyden share the 2026 Nobel Prize?

The Nobel committee does not explain its choices. The prize went to Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel; with only three places, there was no room for Boyden, first author of the 2005 paper that launched optogenetics.

What is the Matthew effect in science?

A term coined by the sociologist Robert Merton in 1968: credit tends to flow to scientists who are already well known. Because it falls even harder on women, the historian Margaret Rossiter called that version the Matilda effect in 1993.

Did Marie Curie almost miss her first Nobel Prize?

Yes. The 1903 nomination named only Henri Becquerel and Pierre Curie. After Gösta Mittag-Leffler alerted Pierre, he wrote asking to be considered together with Marie, and she shared the prize.

Who took Photo 51?

Rosalind Franklin and her PhD student Raymond Gosling, in May 1952, at King’s College London. Maurice Wilkins showed it to James Watson in January 1953 without Franklin’s knowledge.

title.$t: How a Shy Grasshopper Becomes a Locust Swarm

content.$t:
Many will remember the locust swarms that arrived during the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic. Not all grasshoppers are locusts, but every locust was once a grasshopper.

Crowded together, bumping into one another until their serotonin surges, they become locusts, and their all-devouring march to conquer the world is as unstable as it is destructive. A locust swarm is wiped out within a few months, and the survivors take generations to revert to grasshoppers.

As easy as it is for a calm grasshopper to become a locust, returning to being a grasshopper once it has become a locust is far harder.

Grasshopper and locust (from the internet).

In short

  • Locusts are not a separate species: only about a dozen of the world’s roughly 7,000 grasshopper species can turn into locusts.
  • When food runs short and grasshoppers crowd together, their hind legs keep bumping, serotonin surges, and their behavior starts changing within hours.
  • The change is epigenetic, not a mutation: only which part of the DNA gets read changes.
  • A locust lives barely three months; without rain to lay eggs, a swarm collapses on its own.
  • The 2020 swarms reached 55 districts of Nepal but died in the cold hills; in 1996, swarms wiped out crops in Chitwan, Makwanpur, Mahottari and Bara.

Moses, Locusts and the Bible’s Eighth Plague

The Hebrew Bible, written about three thousand years ago, recounts the story of ten plagues that struck Egypt. The Hebrew Bible is Judaism's primary scripture, and its second book, Exodus, tells the story of Moses. The same story of Exodus appears in the first part of the Christian Bible, the Old Testament.

According to the story, Moses worked in the Egyptian palace as an aide to the Pharaoh. One day, he learns that he is not an Egyptian at all but a descendant of the Israelites brought there as slaves. Moses pleads with the Pharaoh to free all the Israelites enslaved in Egypt. But the Pharaoh doesn’t listen; instead, he throws Moses out of the palace.

Moses then rebels against Egypt and frees all the Israelites who had been brought there as slaves. He leads them across the ‘Red Sea’ and through the Arabian Peninsula to Israel. That is the central story of Exodus.

But no story in the world is complete without a revenge.

Before crossing the sea, Moses raises his hand and begs God to punish them all: the rulers of Egypt who enslaved them and the people who tormented them. God hears Moses’s plea and inflicts Egypt with ten plagues.

The river’s water turned to blood. A flood of frogs came, a plague struck the livestock, and hail fell. The eighth plague was locusts.

A wind blew from the east for a day and a night. The next morning, that wind brought such a swarm of locusts that the ground disappeared from view and darkness fell in broad daylight. There was uproar everywhere; every crop was destroyed, and not even the wheat spared by the hail remained.

A locust swarm blotting out the sky (from the internet).

A few days later, the wind shifted, and a west wind swept the locusts away and dropped them into the eastern sea. In the story of Exodus, the locust plague in Egypt ended this way, on its own.

Writing had begun in Egypt some fifteen hundred years before the story of Exodus was written in the Bible. But nowhere in Egypt’s records is a locust plague described. Therefore, this locust story in Exodus should be called a story, not history.

Even so, we can’t say for certain that the Egyptians never saw locusts. Here and there, pictures of grasshoppers are painted in the tombs where they laid their ‘mummies.’ From the pictures alone, it is impossible to tell whether they depict grasshoppers or locusts.

Not all grasshoppers are locusts, but every locust was once a grasshopper.

Today I’ve set out to write about the strange relationship between grasshoppers and locusts. I don’t know how long this piece will be. But if you read to the end, you will find the locust’s whole story.

The First Record of Locusts in History

If we look for locusts not only in stories but also in real history, we have to travel to present-day Iraq, some six hundred years after the Hebrew Bible was written. In the seventh century BCE, Ashurbanipal was king of Assyria (in northern Iraq).

We can still see a scene carved on the wall of his palace from that time.

Ashurbanipal’s palace, the first image of a locust (British Museum, c. 640 BCE).

The king reclines in his garden, drinking wine, with the queen seated beside him. Around them lies a garden of date palms and grapevines. In the garden stands a tree: from one branch hangs the head of the king of Elam (Iran), and on another branch is the image of a locust. Nearby, a bird watches the locust, as if waiting to eat it.

Ashurbanipal used to call Elam’s army ‘a thick swarm of locusts.’ It is thought that the lone locust in the tree was meant to represent the defeated enemy’s army.

In Assyria, investigating and writing about locusts had begun even before Ashurbanipal’s time. Notes recording research on the different stages of locusts, from the palace at Nineveh, appear on tablets dating to a few decades before Ashurbanipal.

Nearly three hundred years after Ashurbanipal, Aristotle wrote about the locust’s life cycle in his book on animals. That book, which classified the locust as a species of its own, remained our main source on locusts for a long time.

The Locust’s Journey to Nepal

Sometimes Egypt. Sometimes Iraq and Assyria. Sometimes Aristotle. And all of it was three thousand years ago. Locusts may seem far away to us, but in our own Nepal, there is a history of locust swarms wiping out crops several times.

Many will still remember locust swarms entering Nepal during the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic. Originating in the Arabian Desert and moving through India, the first swarms entered Nepal on the morning of June 27 at three locations: Rupandehi, Bara, and Sarlahi. More swarms arrived the next day and the day after. On July 12, another swarm entered through Dang and reached as far as Syangja via Pyuthan, Gulmi, and Baglung. On July 16, more arrived through Banke and Kanchanpur, and the swarms that entered through Banke reached as far as Jajarkot via Surkhet and Dailekh.

At that time, locust swarms were seen in 55 of the country’s districts. But the swarms didn’t do much damage to crops. That’s because they headed straight for Nepal’s hills, where the cold air proved deadly to them.

That time, Nepal’s hills wiped out the swarms. But we can’t always count on the hills.

Exactly twenty-four years before the COVID-era swarms, in 1996, locusts entered Nepal through Chitwan. The swarms that came then destroyed nearly 80 percent of the crops in Chitwan, Makwanpur, Mahottari, and Bara. That is the worst destruction locusts have caused in Nepal.

The earliest recorded locust swarms and damage in Nepal’s history date to 1962. At that time, crops in the districts around Kathmandu are said to have been badly damaged. Over the five years from 1926 to 1930, locusts are said to have caused about one hundred million pounds of damage in India. Some sources report that Juddha Shumsher received news at that time of locusts arriving in Nepal’s Tarai.

All three times, the locusts that came to Nepal came from the Arabian Desert. If the locusts in the Exodus story were real, they too must have come from there. Where they ended up depended on the wind: when the east wind blew, they reached Nepal, and when the west wind blew, they reached Egypt.

All the locusts of Asia, Europe, and Africa come from the vast desert belt stretching from West Africa to India. But it would be wrong to think of the locust as a separate species. The calm grasshoppers living all around us are the very locusts that brought the Bible’s plague.

Now let me explain in detail how a grasshopper turns into a locust.

A locust is not a new species or some strange insect.

The Green Insect in the Grass

We have all seen grasshoppers everywhere: on the ridges between rice fields, in grassy meadows, and along the edges of farm plots. Green, the color of grass.

The green insect that lives alone in the grass (from the internet).

Touch one, and it jumps, lands a little way off, and settles again. Catch one and hold it in your hand, and it kicks its legs and, frightened, soon spits a brown juice from its mouth.

A grasshopper does no harm to anyone. It doesn’t destroy anyone’s field. Instead, it becomes food for birds, lizards, and frogs.

It prefers to live alone. If it meets another grasshopper, it moves away. In the morning, it basks in the sun, eats leaves, and hides again.

About 7,000 species of grasshoppers exist worldwide. Most of them spend their lives as loners, meaning they remain grasshoppers forever. They spend their whole lives trying not to be seen, which is why most are the same green as grass. In scientific terms, this solitude-loving nature is called the solitarious phase.

But there are about a dozen grasshopper species that can abandon their solitary nature entirely and enter an aggressive form: the gregarious phase. In other words, they can stop being grasshoppers and become locusts.

A locust is not a new species or some strange insect. In grasshoppers that can become locusts, the DNA is like two different sections of the same book. Read only the grasshopper section of the DNA book, and they stay grasshoppers forever; read the locust section, and they can turn into locusts.

Every Locust Is a Grasshopper, Not Every Grasshopper Is a Locust

When rain falls in the desert, plants sprout everywhere and food is plentiful. Grasshoppers lay eggs, the young grow up, and their numbers rise. While food is plentiful, they follow the desert’s greenery and continue living solitary lives.

And then the rain stops.

The green that was everywhere now survives only in a few patches: here beside a gully, there on damp ground. With food left in only a few places, the grasshoppers start gathering there as well, in search of it.

What we must not forget here is that the grasshoppers didn’t gather in one place because their numbers grew; they were forced together because food was scarce.

Grasshoppers forced together by food shortage (from the internet).

Creatures that prefer to live alone are now forced to crowd together, and a crowd of grasshoppers forms. As they shift and jump, their long hind legs bump into others’ legs. Grabbing a leaf means jostling with another. Amid the shoving and pushing, their legs keep knocking together repeatedly.

It is this very knocking of legs that turns grasshoppers into locusts.

The grasshoppers didn’t gather in one place because their numbers grew; they were forced together because food ran short.

As their long hind legs keep bumping into one another, changes begin inside their bodies. Our bodies have this hormone, too: serotonin. When we are happy, sad, or excited, our bodies make more of it.

The bumping of grasshoppers’ legs multiplies the serotonin in their bodies many times over. What serotonin does in our bodies is still debated, but there is no doubt about its role in a grasshopper.

The Changes That Follow a Serotonin Surge

Within a few hours of serotonin rising in a grasshopper’s body, change begins. Its old habit of living alone starts to shut down completely. In its place, new genes that teach it to live in swarms, become aggressive, and fly nonstop begin to switch on.

Within a few days, the body begins to change.

The green grasshopper molts. The grass-green color disappears, and in its place appear deep yellow, liver-red, and black. It no longer needs to hide, so it no longer needs those colors.

Its wings grow longer, its muscles stronger, and even its brain grows larger. With a long journey ahead, it must move in a crowd, watch what others do, and make more decisions.

These insects are no longer solitary grasshoppers. They have just one purpose now: to advance together and devour whatever lies ahead.

At first, they march across the ground in bands; once their wings grow and they take off in swarms, they become thesame sky-blotting ‘locust swarm’ that brought darkness to Egypt three thousand years ago.

How Does a Serotonin Surge Turn a Grasshopper into a Locust?

Now the question arises: how can serotonin alone produce such an astonishing change in a grasshopper’s body?

To be honest, this tiny chemical’s role is only to carry the news of bumping legs to the cells. Serotonin doesn’t even enter the cells. It stops at the cell membrane, and once the cells recognize it, they begin other changes in the grasshopper’s body.

The serotonin that surges when a grasshopper’s legs bump settles on the cell membrane. There, a protein recognizes serotonin: a G-protein-coupled receptor. On the outside of the cell, the receptor’s mouth recognizes the extra serotonin in the body and binds it.

Once serotonin binds, the receptor’s engine inside the cell switches on. It then sends the news that serotonin has risen through messengers called cyclic AMP (cAMP). Just as a speaker turns up a microphone’s volume so everyone can hear, these messengers amplify the news of rising serotonin many times over inside the cell.

PKA, the Protein Serotonin Switches On

These messengers carry the serotonin signal to another protein, PKA. This PKA protein is the main culprit that turns a grasshopper into a locust. It works in two ways.

Its first job happens instantly, in the nerves. Within the first few minutes of PKA rising in a grasshopper’s body, it begins attaching phosphate to nerve-cell ion channels. Those channels, through which chemicals pass, begin to open. Once the channels loosen, signals travel faster through the nerve cells.

This is what triggers the first behavioral change as a grasshopper turns into a locust. Grasshoppers that haven’t yet become locusts become aggressive, must keep moving, and start seeking company.

Up to this point, nothing has changed in their DNA. All of this is just a simple adjustment to proteins that were already present.

But PKA’s work doesn’t end here.

A few hours of bumping legs is enough to turn a grasshopper into a locust. Turning a locust back into a grasshopper takes generations.

The Biological Change PKA Brings to the Grasshopper

PKA’s second job is the main one. A small piece of it travels to the cell’s center, the nucleus, and brings about biological change to the DNA.

In the book of DNA, closed pages start to open, and open pages start to close.

The small piece of PKA that reaches the nucleus attaches a phosphate to a protein there called CREB. CREB is a transcription factor. Transcription factors are proteins that bind to specific sites on DNA and signal for the genes there to be read. Adding the phosphate should be understood as a signal to start work.

The most important change comes next. Interestingly, the new proteins produced once CREB opens the way carry both types of signals: to close open DNA and to keep closed DNA open. The genes that make a grasshopper now switch off, and the genes a locust needs begin to switch on.

Proteins called DNA methyltransferases switch off the genes needed to be a grasshopper. They add methyl groups to one of the four repeating letters of DNA (A, T, G, C): cytosine (C). Adding methyl groups makes the DNA tighter.

The more methyl groups are added to any part of the DNA, the more tightly that part winds up. The machinery needed for transcription (the process of making RNA from DNA) can’t attach to DNA that has wound up tight, so no RNA or protein is made.

This is one of the things CREB does when it receives the serotonin signal: within a few hours, the genes that the grasshopper’s solitary life depends on begin to switch off.

The genes for being a grasshopper and the genes for being a locust are in the same DNA. Whether it stays a grasshopper or becomes a locust depends on which part of the DNA is read and when. This is where CREB comes in again, switching on another protein called HAT (histone acetyltransferase).

HAT’s job is to attach acetyl groups to DNA. Adding acetyl groups does exactly the opposite of adding methyl groups. The more acetyl groups are added to DNA, the looser that part of the DNA becomes.

The biological process as a grasshopper becomes a locust (made with the help of Claude AI).

In this way, the grasshopper's genes are switched off and the locust's genes are switched on at the same time.

What we need to understand here is that even though the ability to become a locust is present from the start, it is impossible to remain a locust forever. That is why nature works to keep them in the grasshopper state.

A serotonin surge upsets nature’s effort. The padlock on the grasshopper section opens. The first, grasshopper section closes, and the book’s other, locust section begins to be read.

Another important point is that the change from grasshopper to locust is not genetic but epigenetic, shaped by the environment. In other words, no mutation occurs.

Normally, changes in methylation are not passed down from one generation to the next. That biological fact holds true when a locust lays its eggs: the young developing inside the egg develop just like grasshoppers.

But here the locust pulls off another marvel.

Along with her eggs, the mother locust leaves behind a foam-like substance. What exactly this foam is and how it works remain unknown. But because of this foam, the young are born already as aggressive as locusts.

The Locust’s Unstable Life

As terrifying as the swarm’s aggressive, all-devouring march is, it is equally unstable. Look at Nepal itself: the locusts seen in 55 districts in 2020 disappeared on their own within a few months.

A swarm of tens of millions needs a constant supply of food to keep going. An adult locust eats its own weight in food every day. But this boundless hunger becomes the main cause of their downfall.

To avoid starvation, once they have stripped one area of greenery, they are forced to keep flying in search of food. In the end, this great journey ends harshly. Most locusts die exhausted in mid-flight or without finding food along the way.

Such a way of life can never last; the swarm is always on the brink of hunger and crisis. But food shortage is only one reason for their downfall.

First of all, we need to understand that however aggressively they march, as if to wipe out the whole world, locusts are not immortal. Their life cycle is limited: they live only about three months.

In other words, any locust swarm ends within three months, no matter what. Even if no one sprays pesticides, even if the wind doesn’t change, even if food is plentiful. To keep going, locusts have to keep laying new eggs, and that is where their problem begins.

Female locusts can’t lay eggs just anywhere. They need moist sand to lay them. Once the young hatch, they need soft, green plants. Both of these come from one thing: rain.

Without rain, mother locusts can’t lay eggs. Even if they do, the eggs die in dry sand. Even if the young hatch, there is nothing to eat. So a swarm ends not because food runs out but because the next generation fails to survive. The old locusts age and die, and no one is born to take their place.

Another important point: a locust doesn’t fly wherever it likes; it flies with the wind. This usually works because the wind tends to blow toward places where it is raining, and there food is plentiful. In other words, riding the wind is not foolishness; it is a system.

But the system breaks down.

If the wind blows the wrong way, the whole swarm ends up over the sea. There is nowhere to land below; they tire and fall. That is exactly what the Exodus story describes. The episode in which a wind from West Africa swept the locusts that had come to Egypt from the Arabian desert into the sea was not pure imagination. Even today, the same process repeats when locusts strike Egypt.

Why Couldn’t the Locust Swarms Do More Damage in Nepal?

The same thing happened when the last locust swarms arrived in Nepal. Carried by the wind, they reached Nepal’s hills, which acted as a barrier, and the locusts were wiped out.

The locust is a desert insect. It needs warmth. In the cold, its muscles slow down and its flight weakens, and in damp places it contracts fungal disease. The swarms that entered Nepal in 2020 didn’t settle in the Tarai; they headed straight up into the hills. Climbing north from Chitwan, they reached as high as 5,400 meters.

The hills were cold, and the air was very damp. They could neither survive for many days nor lay eggs there. An insect that had flown thousands of kilometers from the Arabian Desert was stopped by our hills.

Any locust swarm is finished within three months, no matter what.

What happens to the surviving locusts after a swarm collapses?

Finally, the most intriguing question: what happens to the locusts that survive after a swarm collapses?

Most locusts die on the journey, but a collapsing swarm doesn’t mean every locust dies. A few survive, and some even lay eggs.

The young that hatch from eggs laid by survivors of a collapsed swarm emerge as locusts for a time. But once the swarm scatters, the bumping of legs stops. No serotonin signal arrives. The padlock on the DNA begins to close again, and the genes that make a locust fall silent.

A few hours of bumping legs is enough to turn a grasshopper into a locust. Turning a locust back into a grasshopper takes generations.

As the crowd thins, the young born from the eggs grow increasingly solitary with each generation, and their young even more so. In this way, after two or three generations, the green color returns, the wings grow shorter, and their nature turns back toward hiding.

After a few generations, they become grasshoppers again. Some scatter back across the same desert, turn green, and start living alone. When there is no swarm, the locust is right there in the desert: few in number, scattered, unnoticed by anyone. This is called the recession period.

In the End, We Are the Locusts’ Story

The final truth is this: an hour is enough to slip unknowingly into a locust crowd. It takes three generations to return to your old form after a locust crowd. And a locust swarm is as unstable as it is terrifying: it is wiped out within three months.

This unstable and destructive journey of the locust may be a mirror of our own society. Last year, stirred by a storm of anger, pain, and conspiracy, did we turn from human beings into locusts? Who knows what invisible ‘serotonin’ whipped up the psychology of our crowd, but we have forgotten the very core of our civilization: ‘Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam,’ the world is one family.

Reading the petty comments on social media, you can see we are busy demonizing one another, exactly like the locusts’ all-devouring march. Social decency and morality are gone; we have forgotten how to be human.

The people who left vulgar, abusive comments and jeers on a video posted by a woman pleading for help in finding her husband, who was lost in a flood, belong to our own society. Just as those who, last year, burned the ward offices, hospitals, and schools of their own villages in revenge were also part of our society.

A locust swarm is wiped out within a few weeks or months. After a few generations, they may even revert to grasshoppers. But as for us, lost like locusts on a journey of cruelty, I have found no grounds to hope that we can become human again.

At a glance: how a grasshopper becomes a locust, and how it turns back.

Grasshoppers and locusts: frequently asked questions

Are locusts and grasshoppers the same?

Every locust is a grasshopper, but not every grasshopper is a locust. Of about 7,000 grasshopper species, only around a dozen can become locusts when crowded.

How does a grasshopper turn into a locust?

When grasshoppers are forced together, their hind legs keep bumping and serotonin rises. Serotonin switches on a protein called PKA, which changes their behavior and, through methyl and acetyl tags on the DNA, switches grasshopper genes off and locust genes on.

How long does a locust swarm last?

A locust lives barely three months. To survive, a swarm must keep laying eggs, and without rain it can’t, so the swarm collapses on its own.

When did locust swarms reach Nepal?

Swarms that came through Chitwan in 1996 caused heavy crop losses. During the 2020 COVID pandemic, swarms reached 55 districts but were stopped by the cold hills.

Can a locust turn back into a grasshopper?

Yes. Once the crowd thins, the bumping stops, serotonin falls, and over two or three generations they become green, solitary grasshoppers again.

This article was first published in Nepali on Shilapatra on September 18, 2026 (Asoj 2, 2083 BS). English translation by the author.

title.$t: एकान्तप्रेमी फट्याङ्ग्रा कसरी सलहको बथान बन्छ?

content.$t:
सन् २०२० को कोरोना माहामारी बेलामा आएको सलहको बथानको संझना धेरैलाई होला। सबै फट्याङ्ग्रा सलह होइनन्। तर, सबै सलह कुनै बेलाका फट्याङ्ग्रा हुन्।

भिडमा, एक आपसमा ठोकिएर सेरोटोनिन बढ्दा सलह बनेका यिनिहरूको संसार जित्ने सर्वभक्षी यात्रा जति विनाशकारी हुन्छ, यिनीहरूको जीवन त्यति नै अस्थिर हुन्छ। सलहको बथान केही महिनामै मासिन्छ, र बाँचेका सलहलाई फेरि फट्याङ्ग्रामा फर्कन पुस्तौँ लाग्छ।

शान्त फट्याङ्ग्रालाई सलह बन्न जति सहज हुन्छ, एकपटक सलह बनिसकेपछी फट्याङ्ग्रामा फर्किन त्यसभन्दा धेरै गाह्रो हुन्छ।

फट्याङ्ग्रा र सलह (इन्टरनेटबाट साभार)

छोटकरीमा

  • सलह छुट्टै प्रजाति होइन; फट्याङ्ग्राका करिब ७ हजार प्रजातिमध्ये एक दर्जनजति मात्र भीडमा सलह बन्न सक्छन्।
  • खाना कम भएर भीड बढ्दा पछाडिका खुट्टा ठोक्किन्छन्, सेरोटोनिन बढ्छ, र केही घण्टामै स्वभाव फेरिन थाल्छ।
  • यो परिवर्तन जिनको उत्परिवर्तन होइन, एपिजेनेटिक हो: डिएनएको कुन भाग पढिने भन्ने मात्र फेरिन्छ।
  • सलह मुस्किलले तीन महिना बाँच्छ; पानी नपरे फुल पार्न नसकेर बथान आफैँ सकिन्छ।
  • सन् २०२० मा ५५ जिल्ला पुगेको बथानलाई नेपालका चिसा पहाडले रोके; सन् १९९६ मा भने चितवन, मकवानपुर, महोत्तरी र बारामा ठूलो क्षति भयो।

मोशा, सलह र बाइबलको आठौँ विपत्तिको कथा

करिब तीन हजार वर्षअघि लेखिएको हिब्रू बाइबलमा इजिप्टमाथि आइपरेका दश विपत्तिको कथा छ। हिब्रू बाइबल यहूदी धर्मको मुख्य ग्रन्थ हो, जसको दोस्रो किताब एक्जोडसमा(Exodus)  मोशा(Moses) को कथा छ। इसाइ बाइबलको पहिलो भाग, ओल्ड टेस्टामेन्टमा पनि एक्जोडसको यही कथा दोहोरिन्छ।

कथाअनुसार, मोशा इजिप्टको दरबारमा फारोको सहयोगी भएर काम गर्थ्यो। एकदिन उसले आफू इजिप्टको नागरिक नभएर त्यहाँ दास बनाएर ल्याइएका इजरायलीको संतान हुँ भनेर थाहा पाउँछ। मोशाले फारोअघि इजिप्टले दास बनाएका सबै इजरायलीहरूलाई मुक्त गर्न बिन्ती गर्छ। तर, उसको बिन्ती फारोले सुन्दैन, उल्टै मोशालाई दरबारबाटै निकालिदिन्छ।

त्यसपछि, मोशाले इजिप्टसँग विद्रोह गर्छ र इजिप्टमा दास बनाएर ल्याइएका सबै इजरायलीहरूलाई दासत्वबाट मुक्त गर्छ। उनीहरूलाई ‘रेड सि’ तारेर अरब प्रायद्वीपको बाटो हुँदै इजरायल लिएर जान्छ। एक्जोडसको मुख्य कथा यही हो।

तर, संसारका कुनै पनि कथा बदलाबिना अपुरो हुन्छ।

समुद्र तर्नु अघि मोशाले हात उठाएर भगवानसँग आफूहरूलाई दास बनाउने इजिप्टका शासक र सताउने जनता सबैलाई सजाय दिन याचना गर्छ। भगवानले मोशाको बिन्ती सुन्छ र इजिप्टमाथि दश विपत्तिको श्राप दिन्छ।

नदीको पानी रगत जस्तो बन्यो। भ्यागुताको बाढी आयो, पशुमा महामारी फैलियो, असिना पर्‍यो। आठौँ विपत्ति सलहको थियो।

पूर्वबाट एक दिन र एक रात बतास चल्यो। अनि त्यो बतासले भोलिपल्ट बिहान सलहको यस्तो बथान ल्यायो कि जमिनको सतह देखिन छाड्यो, दिनदहाडै अँध्यारो भयो। सबैतिर हाहाकार मच्चियो, सबै बालीनाली मासियो, असिनाबाट जोगाएको गहुँसमेत बाँकी रहेन।

सलहको आकाश ढाक्ने बथान (इन्टरनेटबाट साभार)

केही दिनपछि हावा फेरियो र पश्चिमबाट चलेको बतासले सलहलाई बढारेर पूर्वी समुद्रमा खसालिदियो। एक्जोडसको कथामा इजिप्टमा आएको सलहको विपत्ति यसरी आफैँ अन्त्य भएको थियो।

बाइबलमा एक्जोडसको कथा लेखिनुभन्दा करिब पन्ध्र सय वर्ष अघिबाटै इजिप्टमा लेखाइको सुरुवात भइसकेको थियो। तर, इजिप्टका अभिलेखहरूमा कतै पनि सलहको विपत्तिको कथा लेखिएको भेटिँदैन। त्यसैले, एक्जोडसमा लेखिएको सलहको यो कथालाई इतिहास नमानेर कथा नै भन्नुपर्छ।

यद्यपि, इजिप्टका मानिसहरूले सलह कहिल्यै देखेका थिएनन् भनेर किटान गरी भन्न सकिँदैन। उनीहरूको ‘ममी’ राखिएका चिहान-घरहरूमा कतै-कतै फट्याङ्ग्राको चित्र कोरिएको भेटिन्छ। चित्र हेरेर फट्याङ्ग्रा हो कि सलह यकीन छुट्ट्याउन सकिँदैन।

सबै फट्याङ्ग्रा सलह होइनन् तर, सबै सलह कुनै बेलाका फट्याङ्ग्रा हुन्।

आज फट्याङ्ग्रा र सलहको यही अनौठो सम्बन्धबारे लेख्ने सुर कसेको छु। लेख कति लामो हुने हो थाहा छैन। तर, अन्त्यसम्म पढ्नु भयो भने सलहको सम्पूर्ण नालीबेली भेट्टाउनु हुनेछ।

इतिहासमा भेटिएको सलहको पहिलो अभिलेख

सलहलाई कथामा मात्र होइन साँच्चिकै इतिहासमा खोज्ने हो भने हामीले हिब्रू बाइबल लेखिएको करिब छ सय वर्षपछि अहिलेको इराकमा पुग्नुपर्छ। सनपूर्व सातौँ शताब्दीमा अशुर-बनिपाल असिरियाको (उत्तर इराक) राजा थियो।

उसको दरबारको भित्तामा त्यो बेला कुँदिएको एउटा दृश्य हामीले अझै देख्न सक्छौँ।

अशुर-बनिपालको दरबार, पहिलो सलहको चित्र (ब्रिटिस म्युजियम, स.पू. ६४०)

राजा बगैँचामा पल्टिएर रक्सी पिइरहेको छ, रानी छेउमा बसेकी छिन्। वरिपरि खजुर र अङ्गुरको बगैँचा छ। बगैँचामा एउटा रूख छ- एउटा हाँगामा इलमका(इरान) राजाको टाउको झुन्डिएको छ, अर्को हाँगामा सलहको चित्र छ। छेउमा सलहलाई हेरिरहेको एउटा चरा छ, जसले खान कुरेर बसिरहेको झैँ देखिन्छ।

अशुर-बनिपालले इलमको सेनालाई “सलहको बाक्लो हुल” भन्ने गर्थ्यो। त्यसैले रुखमा बसेको एक्लो सलहको माने हारेको शत्रुको फौज देखाउन खोजेको हो भनेर अनुमान गर्ने गरिन्छ।

असिरियामा सलहबारे खोज्न र लेख्न अशुर-बनिपालको समयभन्दा पहिलेबाटै सुरु भइसकेको थियो। असिरियाको निनिभा(Nineveh) दरबारमा सलहको फरक-फरक अवस्थाबारे अनुसन्धान गरेका टिपोटहरू अशुर-बनिपालभन्दा केही दशक पहिले लेखिएका पाटीहरूमा भेटिन्छन्।

अशुर-बनिपालको झन्डै तीन सय वर्षपछि एरिस्टोटलले आफ्नो किताब “एनिमलिया” मा सलहको जीवनचक्रबारे लेखेका थिए। सलहलाई नयाँ प्रजाति बनाएको एरिस्टोटलको त्यही किताब नै लामो समयसम्म सलहबारे हाम्रो मुख्य स्रोत थियो।

सलहको नेपाल यात्रा

कहिले इजिप्ट। कहिले इराक र असिरिया। कहिले एरिस्टोटल। त्यो पनि तीन हजार वर्ष अगाडिका कुरा। हामीलाई सलह टाढाको लाग्न सक्छ। तर, हाम्रै नेपालमा सलहको बथानले कतिपटक बालीनाली सखाप पारेको इतिहास छ।

सन् २०२० को कोरोना महामारी बेला नेपालमा सलहको बथान पसेको सम्झना धेरैलाई अझै होला। अरबको मरुभूमिबाट भारत हुँदै नेपाल आएको सलहको बथान पहिलोपटक जुन २७ बिहान रुपन्देही, बारा र सर्लाही तीन ठाउँबाट नेपाल पसेको थियो। भोलिपल्ट र पर्सिपल्ट अरू बथान आए। जुलाई १२ मा दाङबाट अर्को बथान छिर्‍यो, जुन प्युठान, गुल्मी, बागलुङ हुँदै स्याङ्जासम्म पुग्यो। जुलाई १६ मा बाँके र कञ्चनपुरबाट थपिए, र बाँकेबाट नेपाल छिरेका सलहका बथान सुर्खेत, दैलेख हुँदै जाजरकोटसम्म पुगेका थिए।

त्यो बेला देशका ५५ जिल्लामा सलहको बथान देखिएको थियो। तर, सलहको बथानले बालीनालीमा खासै प्रभाव भने गरेन। किनभने, उनीहरू सिधै नेपालको पहाडतिर लागे, चिसो हावा सलहलाई घातक बन्यो।

त्यतिबेला, नेपालका पहाडले नै सलहको बथानलाई सखाप पारिदिएको थियो। तर, सधैँ पहाडको भर गर्न मिल्दैन।

कोरोना बेला नेपाल भित्रिएका सलहहरू ठ्याक्कै चौबीस वर्ष अघि, सन् १९९६, चितवन हुँदै नेपाल आएका थिए। त्यो बेला नेपाल छिरेका सलहको बथानले चितवन, मकवानपुर, महोत्तरी र बारामा झन्डै ८०% बालीनाली सखाप पारेको थियो। नेपालमा सलहले गरेको सबैभन्दा ठूलो विनाश यही हो।

नेपालको इतिहासमा सलहको बथान र क्षतिबारे सबैभन्दा पुरानो अभिलेख सन् १९६२ मा भेटिन्छ। त्यसबेला काठमाडौँ वरिपरिका जिल्लाहरूमा बालीनालीमा ठूलो क्षति भएको थियो भनिन्छ। सन् १९२६-३० को पाँच वर्ष सलहले भारतमा करिब दश करोड पाउन्डको क्षति गरेको थियो भनिन्छ। त्यही बेला नेपालको तराइमा सलह आएको खबर जुद्ध समसेरले पाएका थिए भनेर कतै-कतै लेखिएको भेटिन्छ।

नेपालमा तीनैपटक आएका सलहहरू अरबको मरुभूमिबाट आएका थिए। यदि एक्जोडसको कथाका सलह साँच्चिकै भए ती पनि यहीँबाट आएको हुनपर्छ। हावाले उनीहरू कहाँ पुग्छन् फरक पार्छ- पूर्वी हावा चल्दा नेपाल आइपुगे, पश्चिमी वायु चल्दा इजिप्ट पुगेका थिए।

एसिया, युरोप र अफ्रिकाका सबै सलहहरू पश्चिम अफ्रिकादेखि भारतसम्म फैलिएको विशाल मरुभूमिय क्षेत्रबाट आउँछन्। यद्यपि हामीले यसो भन्नु गलत हुन्छ, सलह कुनै छुट्टै प्रजाति होइन। हाम्रो वरिपरि बस्ने शान्त फट्याङ्ग्रा नै बाइबलको त्यो बिपत्ती निम्त्याउने सलह हुन्।

फट्याङ्ग्रा कसरी सलह बन्छ, विस्तारमा अब म भन्छु।

सलह कुनै नयाँ प्रजाति वा नौलो कीरा होइन।

घाँसमा बस्ने हरियो कीरा

हामीले खेतको आलीमा, घाँसे मैदानमा, बारीको डिलमा जताततै फट्याङ्ग्रा देखेका छौँ। हरियो, घाँसकै रङको।

घाँसमा एकान्तमा बस्ने हरियो किरा (इन्टरनेटबाट साभार)

हातले छुन खोज्यो उफ्रिहाल्छ, अलि पर गएर फेरि बस्छ। समातेर हातमा राख्यो भने खुट्टा चलाउँछ र केही बेरमा डराएर मुखबाट खैरो रस निकाल्छ।

फट्याङ्ग्राले कसैलाई केही गर्दैन। कसैको खेत सक्दैन। बरु आफैँ चरा, छेपारो र भ्यागुताको खानेकुरा बन्छ।

अनि, यो एक्लै बस्न रुचाउँछ। अरू फट्याङ्ग्रा भेटियो भने टाढिन्छ। बिहान घाम तापेर बस्छ, पात खान्छ, फेरि लुकेर बस्छ।

संसारमा फट्याङ्ग्राका करिब ७ हजार प्रजाति छन्। अधिकांश प्रजातिहरू एकलकाँटे भएर नै जीवन बिताउँछन्, अर्थात् सधैँभरि फट्याङ्ग्रा नै भइरहन्छन्। यिनिहरुको सारा जीवन नदेखिउँ भनेर नै बित्छ, त्यसैले त प्रायः घाँसकै जस्तो हरियो रंगका हुन्छन्। विज्ञानको भाषामा उनीहरूको यो एकान्तप्रेमी स्वभावलाई सोलिटरियस फेज(Solitarious Phase) भनिन्छ।

तर, फट्याङ्ग्राका करिब एक दर्जन प्रजाति यस्ता छन्, जसले यो एकान्तप्रेमी स्वभावलाई चटक्कै छाडेर आक्रामक अवतार- ग्रिगेरियस फेज(Gregarious Phase) धारण गर्ने क्षमता राख्छन्। अर्थात्, यिनीहरू फट्याङ्ग्रा बन्न छाडेर सलह बन्न सक्छन्।

सलह कुनै नयाँ प्रजाति वा नौलो कीरा होइन। सलह बन्न सक्ने फट्याङ्ग्राको डिएनए, एउटै किताबका भिन्न-भिन्न दुई भागझैँ लेखिएको हुन्छ। डिएनएको किताबको फट्याङ्ग्रा बन्ने भाग मात्रै पढे- सधैँ फट्याङ्ग्रा भइरहने, सलहको भाग पढ्न सके- सलहमा परिणत हुन सक्ने।

सबै सलह फट्याङ्ग्रा हुन्- सबै फट्याङ्ग्रा सलह होइनन्

मरुभूमिमा पानी परेको बेला बिरुवा जताततै उम्रिन्छ, खाना प्रशस्त हुन्छ। फट्याङ्ग्राले फुल पार्छ, बच्चा हुर्किन्छन्, सङ्ख्या बढ्छ। खाना प्रशस्त भएको बेला उनीहरू मरुभूमिको हरियो पछ्याएर, एकलकाँटे जीवन नै बाँचिरहेका हुन्छन्।

अनि पानी पर्न छाड्छ।

पहिले जताततै भएको हरियो अब केही टुक्रामा मात्रै बाँकी रहन्छ- कतै खोल्साको छेउ, कतै ओसिलो जमिन। सीमित ठाउँमा मात्रै खाना भएपछि फट्याङ्ग्राहरू पनि खाना खोज्दै त्यहीँ जम्मा हुन थाल्छन्।

यहाँनेर के बिर्सनु हुन्न भने, फट्याङ्ग्राहरूको सङ्ख्या बढेर एक ठाउँमा भेला भएका होइनन्– खानेकुरा कम भएर एक ठाउँमा जम्मा हुन बाध्य भएका हुन्।

खानाको कमिले नजिकिएका फट्याङ्ग्राहरू (इन्टरनेटबाट साभार)

एक्लै बस्न रुचाउने यिनीहरू अब बाध्य भएर एकअर्काको छेउमा आउँछन्, फट्याङ्ग्राको भीड बन्छ। उनीहरूको पछाडिको लामो खुट्टा यताउता गर्दा, उफ्रँदा अर्को फट्याङ्ग्राको खुट्टासँग ठोक्किन्छ। पात खान जाँदा अर्कोसँग जुध्नुपर्छ। घचेटा-घचेटमा पटक-पटक खुट्टा ठोकिरहन्छ।

फट्याङ्ग्राहरूको यही खुट्टा ठोकाइले नै उनीहरूलाई सलहमा परिणत गरिदिन्छ।

फट्याङ्ग्राहरूको सङ्ख्या बढेर एक ठाउँमा भेला भएका होइनन्– खानेकुरा कम भएर एक ठाउँमा जम्मा हुन बाध्य भएका हुन्।

पछाडिको लामा खुट्टा एक-आपासमा बारम्बार जुधिरहँदा उनीहरूको शरीरभित्रै परिवर्तन सुरु हुन्छ। हाम्रो शरीरमा पनि हुन्छ यो हर्मोन- सेरोटोनिन। हामी खुसी, दुखी वा उत्तेजित हुँदा, हाम्रो शरीरले मात्रा बढाएर बनाउँछ।

फट्याङ्ग्राको खुट्टा जुधाइले उनीहरूको शरीरमा सेरोटोनिनको मात्रा कैयौँ गुणाले बढाइदिन्छ। सेरोटोनिनले हाम्रो शरीरमा के गर्छ भन्नेबारे विवाद अझै छ, तर फट्याङ्ग्रा यसले के गर्छ भन्नेबारे कुनै सन्देह छैन।

सेरोटोनिन बढेपछि फट्याङ्ग्रामा आउने परिवर्तन

फट्याङ्ग्राको शरीरमा सेरोटोनिन बढेको केही घन्टामै परिवर्तन सुरु हुन्छ। यिनीहरूको एक्लै बस्ने पुरानो स्वभावलाई पूरै बन्द गर्नतिर लाग्छन्। यसको सट्टा बथानमा बस्न, आक्रामक हुन र निरन्तर उड्न सिकाउने नयाँ जीनहरू सुचारू हुन सुरु हुन्छन्।

केही दिनमै शरीर फेरिन थाल्छ।

हरियो फट्याङ्ग्राको काचुली फेरिन्छ। घाँसे हरियो रङ हराउँछ र त्यसको ठाउँमा गाढा पहेँलो, कलेजी र कालो रङ पलाउँछ। अब लुक्नु छैन, त्यसैले लुक्ने रङ पनि चाहिँदैन।

पखेटा लामो हुन्छ, मांसपेशी बलियो बन्छ, दिमागको आकारसमेत बढ्छ। किनभने अब यसले लामो यात्रा गर्नु छ, भीडमा हिँड्नु छ। अरूको चाल हेर्नु छ, थप निर्णय लिनु छ।

अब ती कीराहरू एक्ला फट्याङ्ग्रा रहेनन्। उनीहरूको एउटै मात्र उद्देश्य हुन्छ- सँगै अघि बढ्ने र अगाडि जे भेटिन्छ, त्यो खर्लप्पै खाइदिने।

सुरुमा जमिनमै बथान बनाएर मार्चपास गर्ने यिनीहरू पखेटा पलाएपछि हुल बनाएर जब उड्न थाल्छन्, तब आकाश ढाक्ने त्यही 'सलहको बथान' बन्छन् जसले तीन हजार वर्षअघि इजिप्टमा अन्धकार ल्याएको थियो।

सेरोटोनिन बढेर फट्याङ्ग्रा कसरी सलह बन्छ?

अब, प्रश्न आउँछ, सेरोटोनिनले गर्दा मात्रै फट्याङ्ग्राको शरीरमा यस्तो अचम्मको परिवर्तन कसरी आउन सक्छ?

साँच्चै भन्नुपर्दा, यो फुच्चे रसायनको भूमिका खुट्टा ठोकिएको खबर कोषहरूसम्म पुर्‍याउने मात्रै हुन्छ। सेरोटोनिन कोषहरूभित्र छिर्न पनि पाउँदैन। यो कोषको झिल्ली (Membrane) मै अड्किन्छ, जसलाई चिनेर फट्याङ्ग्राका शरीरमा कोषहरूले अरू परिवर्तन सुरु गर्छन्।

फट्याङ्ग्रामा खुट्टा ठोकिएर ह्वात्तै बढेको सेरोटोनिन झिल्लीमा आएर बस्छ। त्यहाँ, सेरोटोनिनलाई चिन्ने एकखाले प्रोटिन हुन्छ- जि-प्रोटिन (G-Protein Coupled Receptor)। कोषबाहिर, जि-प्रोटिनको मुखले शरीरमा बढेको सेरोटोनिनलाई चिन्छ र आफूसँग जोड्छ।

सेरोटोनिन जोडिएपछि जि-प्रोटिनको कोषभित्रको इन्जिन सुचारू हुन्छ। जि-प्रोटिन सुचारू भएपछि सेरोटोनिनको मात्रा बढेको खबर साइक्लिक-एएमपीले (cAMP) नाम गरेका हुलाकीहरू मार्फत पठाउँछ। जसरी, स्पिकरले माइक्रोफोनको आवाज बढाएर सबैले सुन्ने गरी ठूलो बनाउँछ- ठीक त्यसरी नै यो हुलाकीले सेरोटोनिन बढेको सूचनालाई कोषभित्र कैयौँ गुणाले बढाइदिन्छ।

सेरोटोनिन बढेर खुल्ने पि.के.ए प्रोटिन

यो हुलाकीले सेरोटोनिन बढेको सङ्केत पि.के.ए (PKA) नाम गरेको अर्को प्रोटिनसम्म पुर्याउँछ। फट्याङ्ग्रालाई सलह बनाउने मुख्य दोषी यही पि.के.ए प्रोटिन हो। यसले दुई किसिमले काम गर्छ।

पहिलो काम स्नायुमा तुरुन्तै हुन्छ। फट्याङ्ग्राको शरीरमा पि.के.एको मात्रा बढेको पहिलो केही मिनेटमै यिनीहरूले स्नायु कोषको आयन (Ion Channel) च्यानलमा फस्फेट जोडिदिन सुरु गर्छन्। रसायन प्रसार हुने ती बाटोहरू खुल्न थाल्छन्। बाटो खुकुलो भएपछि स्नायु कोषहरूमा सङ्केतहरू चाँडो प्रसारण हुन्छन्।

फट्याङ्ग्राबाट सलह बन्दै गर्दा सुरुमा आउने स्वभाव परिवर्तन यही कारणले भएको हुन्छ। अझै सलह नबनिसकेका फट्याङ्ग्राहरू आक्रामक बन्छन्, हिँडिरहनुपर्छ, साथी खोज्न थाल्छन्।

यहाँसम्म यिनीहरूको डिएनएमा केही जैविक परिवर्तन भएको हुँदैन। यो सबै पहिले नै भएको प्रोटिनहरूमा भएको सामान्य फेरबदल मात्रै हो।

तर, पि.के.एको काम यतिमै सीमित छैन।

फट्याङ्ग्रालाई सलह बन्न केही घण्टा खुट्टा ठोकिए पुग्छ। सलहबाट फट्याङ्ग्रा बन्न पुस्तौँ लाग्छ।

पि.के.एले फट्याङ्ग्रामा ल्याउने जैविक परिवर्तन

पिकेएको दोस्रो काम मुख्य हुन्छ। यसको सानो टुक्रा, कोषको केन्द्र, न्युक्लियसमा पुग्छ र डिएनएमा जैविक परिवर्तन ल्याइदिन्छ।

डिएनएको किताबमा पहिले बन्द भएको पाना खुल्न थाल्छ र खुला पाना बन्द हुन सुरु हुन्छ।

कोषको केन्द्रमा पुगेको पि.के.एको सानो टुक्राले त्यहाँ भएको क्रेब (CREB) प्रोटिनमा फस्फेटको टुक्रा जोडिदिन्छ। क्रेब एक किसिमको ट्रान्सक्रिप्सन फ्याक्टर हो। ट्रान्सक्रिप्सन फ्याक्टर भन्नाले डिएनएको निश्चित ठाउँमा गएर बस्ने र त्यहाँको जिन पढ्न इशारा दिने प्रोटिन हुन्। फस्फेटको जोडाइको अर्थ काम गर्न सुरु गर भनेर सङ्केत दिएको बुझ्नुपर्छ।

सबैभन्दा महत्त्वपूर्ण परिवर्तन त्यसपछि आउँछ। रोचक त के छ भने, क्रेबले बाटो खोलेर बनेका नयाँ प्रोटिनहरूले दुवै खाले- खुला डिएनएलाई बन्द गर्ने र बन्द डिएनएलाई खुला राख्ने सङ्केत बोकेका हुन्छन्। फट्याङ्ग्रा बनाउने जिनहरू अब बन्द हुन्छन् र सलहलाई चाहिने जीनहरू खुल्न थाल्छन्।

फट्याङ्ग्रा बन्न चाहिने जिनहरू बन्द गर्ने काम डिएनए मिथाइलट्रान्सफरेज (DNA Methyl Transferase) नाम गरेका प्रोटिनले गर्छ। यसले, डिएनएका दोहोरिरहने चारवटा अक्षरहरू (A T G C) मध्ये एक- साइटोसिनमा(C) मिथाइलका अणुहरू थपिदिन्छ। मिथाइल थपिनु भनेको डिएनएलाई कसिलो बनाउनु हो।

डिएनएको कुनै पनि भागमा मिथाइलका अणुहरू जति थपिँदै जान्छन्, डिएनए त्यति नै खुम्चिँदै जान्छ। डिएनएको खुम्चिएर कसिलो भएको भागमा ट्रान्सक्रिप्सनका (डिएनए बाट आरएनए बन्ने प्रक्रिया) लागि चाहिने संयन्त्र जोडिन सक्दैन, आरएनए र प्रोटिन बन्दैन।

सेरोटोनिनको सङ्केत पाएर क्रेब प्रोटिनले गर्ने एउटा काम यही हो, फट्याङ्ग्राको एकलकाँटे जीवनलाई चाहिने जिनहरू केही घन्टामै बन्द हुन सुरु हुन्छन्।

फट्याङ्ग्रा बन्न चाहिने जिन र सलह बन्न चाहिने जिन एउटै डिएनएमा हुन्छन्। फट्याङ्ग्रा बनिरहने कि सलह बन्ने फरक डिएनएको कुन भाग कहिले पढिन्छ भन्नेमा हुन्छ। यहाँनेर क्रेब प्रोटिनले नै काम गरेको हुन्छ, जसले “ह्याट” (Histone Acetyl Transferase) नाम गरेको अर्कोथरी प्रोटिनलाई खोलिदिन्छ।

“ह्याट”को काम डिएनएमा एसिटाइलका अणुहरू जोडिदिनु हो। एसिटाइलका अणुहरू जोडिँदा मिथाइल जोडाइको ठ्याक्कै उल्टो हुन्छ। डिएनएमा जति धेरै एसिटाइलका अणुहरू थपियो, डिएनएको त्यो भाग त्यति नै खुकुलो हुँदै जान्छ।

फट्याङ्ग्राबाट सलह बन्दा हुने जैविक प्रक्रिया (क्लाउड एआइको सहयोगले बनाएको)

यसरी फट्याङ्ग्रालाई चाहिने जिनहरू बन्द हुने र सलहलाई चाहिने जिनहरू खुल्ने काम एकैसाथ भइरहेको हुन्छ।

यहाँनेर हामीले के बुझ्नुपर्छ भने सलह बन्ने क्षमता पहिलेबाटै भए पनि सधैँ सलह बनेर बस्न सम्भव छैन। प्रकृतिले त्यही कारण यिनीहरूलाई फट्याङ्ग्रा अवस्थामा राख्न जोड गर्छ।

प्रकृतिको यो प्रयासलाई सेरोटोनिनको मात्रा बढेर बिथोलिदिन्छ। सलह बन्ने भागमा लागेको भोटे ताल्चा खुल्छ। फट्याङ्ग्रावाला पहिलो भाग बन्द हुन्छ र किताबको सलहवाला अर्को भाग पढ्न सुरु हुन्छ।

अर्को महत्त्वपूर्ण कुरा के छ भने, फट्याङ्ग्राबाट सलह बन्दा उनीहरूमा भएको परिवर्तन आनुवंशिक (Genetic) होइन, वातावरण अनुकूलित (Epigenetic) हो। अर्थात् कुनै उत्परिवर्तन (Mutation) भएको हुँदैन।

सामान्यतया मिथाइलेसनमा आएका परिवर्तनहरू एक पुस्ताबाट अर्को पुस्तामा सरेर जाँदैनन्। सलहले फुल पार्दै गर्दा जीवविज्ञानको यो तथ्य त सत्य हुन्छ, फुलभित्र हुर्किने बच्चा फट्याङ्ग्रा जसरी नै विकास भएको हुन्छ।

तर, यहाँनेर सलहले अर्को अचम्म गर्छ।

माउ सलहले फुलको साथमा फिँजजस्तो अरू कुरा पनि छाड्छे। यो फिँजस्तो पदार्थ के हो, ठ्याक्कै कसरी काम गर्छ, हामीले थाहा पाउन अझै बाँकी छ। तर, यही फिँजको कारण नयाँ बच्चाहरू जन्मँदै सलहजस्तै आक्रामक भएरै जन्मिन्छन्।

सलहको अस्थिर जीवनकाल

सलहको बथानले गर्ने आक्रामक र सर्वभक्षी यात्रा जति भयानक हुन्छ, त्यति नै अस्थिर पनि हुन्छ। नेपालमै हेरौँ। सन् २०२० मा ५५ जिल्लामा देखिएको सलह केही महिनामा आफैँ हरायो।

करोडौँको सङ्ख्यामा उड्ने सलहको बथान चलिरहन निरन्तर खाना चाहिन्छ। एउटा वयस्क सलहले हरेक दिन आफ्नो तौल बराबरको खाना खान्छ। तर, यही असीमित भोक नै उनीहरूको पतनको मुख्य कारण बन्छ।

भोकमरीबाट बच्न एउटा क्षेत्रको हरियाली सखाप पारेपछि खाना खोज्दै निरन्तर उडिरहन बाध्य हुन्छन्। अन्ततः यो महायात्राको अन्त्य निकै कठोर हुन्छ। धेरैजसो सलहहरू उड्दा-उड्दै थाकेर वा बाटोमा खाना नभेटेर मर्छन्।

सलहको यस्तो जीवनशैली कुनै पनि हालतमा दिगो हुँदैन; बथान सधैँ भोक र सङ्कटको किनारमा हुन्छ। तर, खानाको अभाव उनीहरूको पतनको एउटामात्रै कारण भने होइन।

सबैभन्दा पहिलो त, हामीले के बुझ्नुपर्छ भने संसारै सखाप पार्छु झैँ जति आक्रामक भएर हिँडे पनि सलहहरू अमर होइनन्। उनीहरूको जीवनचक्र सीमित हुन्छ- मुस्किलले तीन महिना बाँच्छन्।

अर्थात्, सलहको कुनै पनि बथान तीन महिनाभित्रै सकिन्छ, चाहे केही नहोस्। कसैले औषधि नछर्के पनि, हावा नफेरिए पनि, खाना प्रशस्त भए पनि। सलहहरू टिकिरहन नयाँ फुल पारिरहनुपर्छ, र उनीहरूको समस्या यहीँबाट सुरु हुन्छ।

पोथी सलहले जहाँ पायो त्यहीँ फुल पार्न सक्दिनन्। फुल पार्न ओसिलो बालुवा चाहिन्छ। फुलबाट बच्चा निस्किएपछि तिनका लागि मुलायम हरियो बिरुवा चाहिन्छ। यी दुवै एउटै कुरा पानीबाट आउँछन्।

पानी परेन भने माउ सलहले फुल पार्न सक्दिनन्। पार्‍यो भने पनि सुक्खा बालुवामा फुल मर्छ। बच्चा निस्के पनि खाने केही हुँदैन। त्यसैले बथान सकिनुको कारण खाना सकिनु होइन, वंश नचल्नु हो। पुराना सलह बुढा हुन्छन्, मर्छन्, र तिनको ठाउँ लिने कोही जन्मँदैन।

अनि अर्को महत्त्वपूर्ण कुरा- सलह आफूखुसी उड्दैन, हावाकै दिशामा उड्छ। यो प्रयासले सामान्यतया काम गर्छ, किनभने हावा प्रायः पानी परिरहेको ठाउँतिरै बग्छ र त्यहाँ खाना प्रशस्त हुन्छ। अर्थात्, हावाको भरमा उड्नु मूर्खता होइन, एउटा प्रणाली हो।

तर, प्रणाली बिग्रन्छ।

हावा गलत दिशामा लाग्यो भने पूरै बथान समुद्रमाथि पुग्छ। तल बस्ने ठाउँ हुँदैन, थाक्छ, र खस्छ। एक्जोडसको कथामा पनि यही लेखिएको थियो। अरबको मरुभूमिबाट इजिप्ट आएका सलहलाई, पश्चिम अफ्रिकाबाट आएको बतासले बढारेर समुद्रमा लगेको प्रसङ्ग सम्पूर्ण कल्पना थिएन। इजिप्टमा सलहले आक्रमण गर्दा अहिले पनि बारम्बार यही प्रक्रिया नै दोहोरिरहन्छ।

नेपालमा सलहको बथानले किन धेरै विनाश गर्न सकेन त?

नेपालमा पछिल्लोपटक सलहको बथान आउँदा पनि यस्तै भएको थियो। हावाको तालमा उनीहरू नेपालको पहाडमा पुगे, जसले पर्खाल बनेर काम गर्‍यो र सलह सखाप भए।

सलह मरुभूमिको कीरा हो। यसलाई न्यानो चाहिन्छ। चिसोमा यसको मांसपेशी सुस्ताउँछ, उडाइ घट्छ, र चिस्यान बढी भएको ठाउँमा ढुसीजन्य रोग लाग्छ। सन् २०२० मा नेपाल पसेका बथान तराईमा बसेनन्, एकैपटक माथि पहाडतिर लागे। ती चितवनबाट उत्तरतिर उक्लिँदै ५,४०० मिटरसम्म पुगे।

पहाड चिसो थियो र हावामा चिस्यान धेरै थियो। तिनले न धेरै दिन बाँच्न सके, न त्यहाँ फुल पार्न। अरबको मरुभूमिबाट हजारौँ किलोमिटर उडेर आएको कीरालाई हाम्रा पहाडले रोकिदिए।

सलहको कुनै पनि बथान तीन महिनाभित्रै सकिन्छ, चाहे केही नहोस्।

सलहको बथान मासिएपछि बाँचेका सलहको के हुन्छ?

र, अन्त्यमा सबैभन्दा रोचक प्रश्न- बथान मासिएपछि पनि बाँचेका सलहको के हुन्छ?

अधिकांश सलहहरू यात्रामै मर्छन्। तर, सलहको बथान मासिनु भनेको सबै सलह मर्नु भने होइन। केही बाँचेका हुन्छन्, कसैले फुल पनि पार्छन्।

बथान सकिएर बाँचेका सलहले पारेको फुलबाट निस्किएका बच्चाहरू केही समयसम्म सलह जसरी नै निस्कन्छन्। तर, बथान छरिएपछि खुट्टामा ठोक्किने बन्द हुन्छ। सेरोटोनिनको सङ्केत आउँदैन। डिएनएको भोटे ताल्चा फेरि लाग्न सुरु हुन्छ, र सलह बनाउने जिनहरू चुप लाग्दै जान्छन्।

फट्याङ्ग्रालाई सलह बन्न केही घण्टा खुट्टा ठोकिए पुग्छ। सलहबाट फट्याङ्ग्रा बन्न पुस्तौँ लाग्छ।

भीड घट्दै गएपछि फुलबाट निस्केका बच्चा पुस्तैपिच्छे अलि बढी एक्लो स्वभावका भएर जन्मन्छन्। तिनका बच्चा अझ बढी। यसरी दुई-तीन पुस्तापछि फेरि हरियो रङ पलाउँछ, पखेटा छोटो हुन्छ, र स्वभाव फेरि लुक्नेतिर फर्किन्छ।

केही पुस्तापछि उनीहरू फेरि फट्याङ्ग्रा नै बन्न थाल्छन्। कोही फर्केर उही मरुभूमिमा छरिन्छन्, हरियो हुन्छन्, र एक्लै बस्न थाल्छन्। बथान नभएको बेला सलह त्यहीँ मरुभूमिमा नै हुन्छ- थोरै, छरिएर, कसैलाई थाहै नहुने गरी। यसलाई विश्रामकाल (recession) भनिन्छ।

अन्त्यमा, हामी सलहको कथा

अन्तिम सत्य यही हो, अन्जानमा सलहको भीडमा पस्न एक घण्टा भए पुग्छ। सलहको भीडबाट पुरानै स्वरूपमा फर्किन तीन पुस्ता लाग्छ। अनि सलहको बथान जति भयानक हुन्छ त्यति नै अस्थिर हुन्छ- तीन महिनामै मासिन्छ।

सलहको यो अस्थिर र विनाशकारी यात्रा, सायद हाम्रो समाजको ऐना हो। गत वर्ष रिस, पीडा र षड्यन्त्रको हुरीले उद्वेलित हुँदा, हामी कतै मान्छेबाट सलह त बनेनौँ? हाम्रो भिडको मनोविज्ञानलाई कुन अदृश्य 'सेरोटोनिन'ले उकास्यो कुन्नि, हामीले हाम्रो सभ्यताको मूल मर्म, 'वसुधैव कुटुम्बकम्' नै बिर्सिसकेका छौँ।

सामाजिक सञ्जालमा तुच्छ कमेन्टहरू हेर्दा देखिन्छ, एक-अर्कालाई दानवीकरण गर्न हामी मस्त छौँ- ठ्याक्कै सलहको सर्वभक्षी यात्रा जस्तै। सामाजिक मर्यादा र नैतिकता हराइसकेको छ, हामी मान्छे बन्न बिर्सेका छौँ।

बाढीमा हराएको श्रीमान् खोज्न आग्रह गर्दै एकजना महिलाले हालेको भिडियोमा आमचाकरी कमेन्ट र अट्टहास गर्नेहरू हाम्रै समाजका हुन्। जसरी, प्रतिशोधका लागि गत वर्ष आफ्नै गाउँका वडा कार्यालय, हस्पिटल र विद्यालय जलाउने पनि हाम्रो समाजका थिए।

सलहको बथान त केही हप्ता, महिनामै मासिन्छ। केही पुस्तापछि उनीहरू फट्याङ्ग्रामा फर्किन पनि सक्छन्। तर, सलह जस्तै दानवीयताको यात्रामा हराएका हामी, फेरि मानिस बन्न सक्छौँ कि नाइँ, आशा गर्ने आधार मैले भेटाएको छैन।

एक नजरमा: फट्याङ्ग्रा कसरी सलह बन्छ, र फेरि कसरी फर्कन्छ।

सलह र फट्याङ्ग्राबारे धेरैले सोध्ने प्रश्न

के सलह र फट्याङ्ग्रा एउटै हुन्?

सबै सलह फट्याङ्ग्रा हुन्, तर सबै फट्याङ्ग्रा सलह होइनन्। करिब ७ हजार प्रजातिमध्ये एक दर्जनजति फट्याङ्ग्रा मात्र भीडमा सलह बन्न सक्छन्।

फट्याङ्ग्रा सलह कसरी बन्छ?

खाना कम भएर एकै ठाउँ थुप्रिँदा पछाडिका खुट्टा ठोक्किन्छन्, सेरोटोनिन बढ्छ। सेरोटोनिनले पि.के.ए प्रोटिन सक्रिय गर्छ, जसले स्वभाव फेर्छ र मिथाइल र एसिटाइलको चिनोमार्फत फट्याङ्ग्राका जिन बन्द र सलहका जिन खोलिदिन्छ।

सलहको बथान कति दिन टिक्छ?

सलह मुस्किलले तीन महिना बाँच्छ। बथान टिक्न नयाँ फुल पारिरहनुपर्छ, तर पानी नपरे फुल पार्न सक्दैन, त्यसैले बथान आफैँ सकिन्छ।

नेपालमा सलहको बथान कहिले आएको थियो?

सन् १९९६ मा चितवन हुँदै आएको बथानले ठूलो क्षति गर्‍यो। सन् २०२० मा कोरोना महामारीको बेला आएको बथान ५५ जिल्लामा देखियो, तर चिसा पहाडले रोके।

सलह फेरि फट्याङ्ग्रा बन्न सक्छ?

सक्छ। भीड घटेपछि खुट्टा ठोक्किन छाड्छ, सेरोटोनिन घट्छ, र दुई–तीन पुस्तामा फेरि हरियो, एकान्तप्रेमी फट्याङ्ग्रा बन्छन्।

यो लेख पहिलो पटक २०८३ असोज २ गते शिलापत्रमा प्रकाशित भएको थियो।
