title.$t: How a Salamander Regrows Its Limbs

content.$t:
A gecko makes a copy of its tail. The thakthake, the salamander of Nepal’s eastern hills, can rebuild a severed leg just as it was, with bone, nerves and toes. The same instructions are in our DNA too, but after birth they are locked away.

This article was first published in Nepali on Shilapatra on August 11, 2026 (Saun 26, 2083 BS). This is the author’s own English translation. Read the original: https://shilapatra.com/detail/192284

How the thakthake regrows a severed leg, at a glance.

How I Met the Salamander at School

I first came across the salamander as a child. It was during my school days: on the break after my sixth-grade exams, I started rummaging through the bookshelf at home. That was when I found an old science magazine in Hindi.

I don’t remember the magazine’s name; I’ve forgotten the title of the story and the hero’s name, too. It was about a scientist who had lost his arms and legs in an accident and experimented on himself, using the salamander’s ability to regrow lost body parts. I don’t even remember whether the biologist succeeded or failed in the end. But that is where my bond with the salamander began.

It was this astonishing ability of the salamander that awakened in me the urge to study biology. For a long time after reading the story, I assumed that salamanders regrowing severed limbs was just the writer’s imagination. Only when I studied salamanders in plus-two did I learn that they really do have an astonishing power to heal. Cut off a salamander’s arm, leg, tail, or other body part, and within a few months it can grow back just as it was.

Transferring that ability from the salamander to a human, as in the story, really is just imagination, like that Lizard villain from Spider-Man.

The Salamander and the House Gecko Are Not the Same

Until I finished school, I believed the salamander was a cousin of the house gecko; after all, the gecko grows a new tail, too. But far from being cousins, the two don’t even belong to the same animal class.

House geckos and lizards are reptiles: they have dry, scaly skin, lay eggs, and are born and grow up on land. The salamander is a relative of the frog, an amphibian: it has slippery skin, lays its eggs in water, and its young grow up in water like tadpoles.

That both the salamander and the gecko can regrow a lost tail isn’t because they are related; it’s a coincidence arrived at by two different paths. And the tail a gecko grows back isn’t its old tail either, but more on that later.

The Salamander, or Maipokhari’s Thakthake

Only much later did I learn that the salamander was not just a creature in some faraway book. It is found in great numbers in Maipokhari, in our own Ilam. It is about twenty centimeters long, with rough black skin and orange markings. Its head resembles a crocodile’s, with bony ridges along its flanks. Because its head and body look so much like a crocodile’s, the thakthake is also called the crocodile newt.

There are about eight hundred species of salamander worldwide. The newt, the salamander found in Europe and most studied, looks much like ours. But there are many other kinds of salamander: the axolotl of Mexico lives its whole life in its juvenile form. The giant salamanders of Japan and China grow up to one and a half meters long; they are the largest amphibians in the world. Maipokhari’s thakthake is a relative of all of them, and it has the same ability.

Locals in Nepal’s Ilam and Panchthar, in Darjeeling, and around Bhutan already knew this salamander as the thakthake. But only ten years ago did we learn that our thakthake is not the same as the salamander found in Burma and China (Tylototriton verrucosus).

In July 2014, Janak Raj Khatiwada, Shanta Paudel, and Subarna Ghimire collected a few specimens from Maipokhari. Comparing their morphology and DNA confirmed that this was a salamander species new to science. In 2015, Khatiwada’s team introduced it to the world as Tylototriton himalayanus.

Maipokhari’s thakthake is found only in Ilam and Panchthar, Darjeeling, and western Bhutan, at elevations of roughly nine hundred to two thousand six hundred meters. It is also the only salamander species found in Nepal.

Does a Gecko Grow Back the Same Tail?

A gecko’s tail doesn’t break off by itself; the gecko drops it. If a cat chases it or someone grabs its tail, it contracts its muscles and simply leaves the tail behind. This is where the difference between the salamander and the gecko begins.

A gecko’s tail doesn’t break just anywhere. A weak line is already built into the tail’s bones, and the tail breaks only along that line. The blood vessels also have points that can be sealed shut. As soon as the tail comes off, those points seal and block the flow of blood, so the gecko doesn’t bleed when it drops its tail.

The dropped tail thrashes on the ground for a few minutes. Even after it separates from the body, its nerves and muscles continue to work for a while. This draws the predator’s attention, and the gecko escapes.

The new tail is not the old one; it is only a copy. The old bone inside the tail doesn’t return. Instead of bone, a long tube of cartilage forms. The joint knobs don’t form as before, and the spinal nerve doesn’t fully return. You can tell just by looking: the scales are a different color, and the new tail is shorter than before. And a gecko can never drop its tail a second time from the same spot. The weak line where the tail breaks exists only in bone, not in the new cartilage tube.

The only Nepali creature with the ability I read about still lives in Maipokhari, Ilam. The thakthake, which still knows how to read the instructions we have forgotten, must surely have come down to the pond again this year.

The gecko makes something else that looks like a tail; the salamander restores the original structure of its cells.

What Happens When We Get Hurt?

A week ago, while opening a carton of supplies that had arrived at the lab, I nicked myself with a paper knife. The blood from the cut above the nail of my index finger stopped within a few minutes, but the mark is still visible.

When my finger was cut, the body first tried to stop the bleeding. Then immune cells arrived to clear dirt and germs from around the wound. Next, fibroblasts began weaving collagen threads to close the wound. A few days later, the weave tightened and the wound closed, but a scar remained where it had been cut.

When we are wounded, the newly formed scar can never become like the skin it once was. In healthy skin, the collagen mesh spreads evenly in every direction, woven like a spider’s web or a fishing net. When a wound is patched, new collagen is added, but it is not arranged as before. In the rush to close the wound, collagen piles up everywhere without structure. Hair doesn’t grow on a scar, it doesn’t sweat, and you can’t even feel it when it’s touched.

There is a reason the body chooses this route. Rebuilding skin to its original state takes weeks, and for all those days there is a risk of infection. Even so, we haven’t entirely lost the salamander’s kind of healing. Even if two-thirds of the liver is removed, the remaining tissue grows back to its original weight within a few weeks, though not to its original shape. If a small child’s fingertip is cut off above the base of the nail, it can grow back, bone, skin, and nail. And if an embryo is wounded in the first months in the mother’s womb, the wound heals without a scar.

It isn’t that we never had the salamander’s ability. As we grow up, this ability gradually fades away; the salamander retains it throughout its life.

From One Cell to a Whole Body

Every animal that reproduces sexually, like us, begins as a single cell. That cell divides into two, then four, then eight. Within a few days, a small ball of cells forms: the morula. Up to this point, all the cells are alike. None of them yet knows what it will become; each can become anything.

As the morula continues dividing, it first becomes a blastula. The cells now begin to determine what they will become. As the embryo grows, three layers separate. The outermost layer becomes skin and nerves. The middle layer becomes bone, muscle, heart, and blood. The inner layer becomes the gut, lungs, and liver. The cells that build arms and legs come from the middle layer.

In most animals, once cells have chosen what to become, there is no going back; once a cell has become a heart cell, it can never become a skin cell again.

How Does a Salamander Regrow a Leg?

When we are wounded, our bodies rush to close the wound by producing as much collagen as possible. The salamander does exactly the opposite.

When a salamander’s leg is cut off, within the first few minutes, skin cells begin moving in from the edges. Within twelve hours, a thin layer has formed over the wound. No blood clots into a scab as it does in us; from the start, the wound is covered by skin-like cells. The newly formed cells over the stump continue to send chemical signals to the fibroblasts underneath. The rush to patch the wound with a jumbled mesh of collagen, as happens in humans, never even gets started.

An even more astonishing change occurs in the cells around the wound. The nearby muscle, bone, and cartilage give up their identity. They forget they are muscle and revert to an embryonic state. The cells then gather at the wound to form a small mound: the blastema. Here, the salamander defies the established rule that once the three layers separate during embryonic development, there is no going back.

For a salamander to form a blastema, blood vessels are needed; without immune cells, the healing process cannot even begin. Even after the injury, the blood vessels continue to deliver the same chemicals to the salamander as before. These chemicals tell the cells of the newly formed blastema to keep dividing.

If the nerves are severed along with the salamander’s leg, none of this process can begin. Not every blastema cell can become anything, though; the old cells can only revert to their former role in their former place. A cell that came from muscle becomes muscle again, one from cartilage becomes cartilage. Skin becomes skin, nerve becomes nerve.

As the blastema grows, the work left off in the embryo resumes. The blastema reactivates the leg-building genes. The salamander hasn’t found a new method; it has simply started reading its own old instructions again, just as before. As in the embryo, the cells divide again: some become bone, some muscle, some nerve, some skin.

The salamander hasn’t found a new method; it has simply started reading its own old instructions again.

And these cells also know where they are in the leg. As a leg forms in the embryo, every cell carries its own address: how far it is from the shoulder. That address isn’t erased even after the animal grows up. The blastema has no picture of the leg it must build, only addresses. The cells at the cut read their address and then build whatever is missing below it. That is why a cut at the wrist grows back only a hand, while a cut at the shoulder grows back the whole leg from the shoulder down.

It takes a salamander one or two months to regrow a leg, and a large salamander even longer. At first, the new leg is smaller than the old one, then it slowly grows to full size. The new leg isn’t a copy like the gecko’s tail: bone where bone should be, joints where joints should be, and the same number of fingers as before.

But even the salamander’s regenerative ability has limits. It rebuilds only outward from the cut: legs, tails, and jaws regrow. If the same spot is cut repeatedly, the new leg slowly stops forming as before: fewer fingers, sometimes crooked. Salamanders can heal injuries to the head or heart, but if the head or body is cut off, they die too.

Why Can’t Our Bodies Heal Like a Salamander’s?

Our blood is warm, and bacteria multiply quickly in that warmth. So the longer a wound stays open, the greater the risk. Our immune system is built with that in mind: as soon as we are injured, inflammation sets in, recruiting neutrophils and macrophages, and on their signal, fibroblasts rush to close the wound.

A salamander is cold-blooded and lives in cold water. In that environment, bacteria can’t multiply as quickly as they do in our bodies, so leaving a wound open for a few weeks isn’t as risky. When a salamander is injured, macrophages arrive first, but they rush to release chemicals that calm inflammation rather than to close the wound. The wound stays calm, and in that calm, the blastema forms and the wound begins to fill. In the lab, if macrophages are removed, salamanders scar just like we do.

Where Is That Locked-Away Key?

We have the genes salamanders need to heal, too. The genes switched on in the blastema aren’t new; salamanders didn’t invent them. When we were embryos, those same genes helped build our arms. As our bodies developed, they were simply switched off, bit by bit.

Every cell in our body carries the same DNA. A skin cell has the genes for building a heart; a heart cell has the genes for building skin. The difference lies not in which genes a cell carries, but in which are switched on and which are switched off.

Genes are switched off by chemical tags placed on a chromosome’s DNA. Whether small molecules called methyl are attached to the DNA determines which genes are off and which are on. Where there is a lot of methyl, the DNA is wound tightly around spools of protein called histones, and the gene-reading machinery can’t even reach it. Only genes in open stretches with few methyl molecules attached can be used to make RNA and protein.

In us, once the body is built, the embryonic genes are switched off in just this way. The methyl tags go on, the DNA winds up tight, and each cell gets on with its own job. Once genes are switched off, the tags are passed on through cell division to the next cell: skin stays skin, heart stays heart.

In us, this heavy padlock on those genes doesn’t unlock when we’re injured. Genes do switch on in our wounds, but they are genes for making collagen, not for building an arm.

In salamanders, these tags come off after an injury. Proteins that remove methyl groups become active in the wound cells, the tightly wound DNA begins to open, and genes that were switched off since the embryo are read again. This is what it means for a cell to give up its identity: the DNA hasn’t changed; the lock on it has been opened.

The DNA hasn’t changed; the lock on it has been opened.

The DNA is the same in both; the difference lies in which parts can be read. When we talk about this lock, we also have to look at the salamander’s genome.

A salamander’s DNA is ten times larger than ours. We have three billion nucleotides; the axolotl, the salamander of Mexico, has thirty-two billion. Its number of chromosomes, though, is smaller than ours: we have 46, it has 28. The axolotl’s 28 chromosomes are far larger than ours, yet its number of genes is about the same as ours. All the extra DNA sits between the genes, as long stretches of repeating letters. It is the DNA between the genes that decides which gene switches on when.

The axolotl’s genome is ten times larger than ours, yet it has just as many genes. And for all that DNA, the salamander has no magic gene we lack. The difference is that a huge genome means large cells, and large cells divide slowly. That is one reason it takes a salamander months to grow a new leg.

Because salamander cells divide less often, their risk of cancer is relatively low. So salamanders can afford to keep those genes unlocked, whereas ours are locked to guard against cancer. Both of us have the genes that switch on in the blastema; the difference lies in when they switch on and when they switch off.

So What Are Scientists Doing Now?

The axolotl’s full genome was sequenced only in 2018. Afterward, we learned how blastema cells remember their address: a certain protein is abundant in cells near the shoulder and scarce in cells near the fingers. In the lab, if that protein is boosted, a blastema that was about to grow just a hand starts growing a whole arm.

The salamander’s ability is being tested in mice as well. When a fingertip is cut off and a protein similar to the salamander’s is boosted there, part of it has grown back, bone and nail included, instead of scarring.

But we need to think carefully about transferring the salamander’s ability to humans. The very inflammation that is suppressed to prevent scarring is also what keeps infection at bay. And the very lock that is opened to make cells give up their identity, if left open, lets cells divide out of control and turn into cancer.

That is why today’s work is not aimed at regrowing an entire arm. Healing stubborn wounds in diabetic patients without scarring, restoring sweat glands to burned skin, and turning the scar left in the heart after a heart attack back into muscle: these are the small steps being taken.

And, That Story

Thinking about that story today, it seems to me it was a Spider-Man comic retold in Hindi. That was exactly what Spider-Man’s Dr. Curt Connors was after, too. Having lost an arm in an accident, he tried lizard genes on himself. The arm did grow back. But lizard genes give only what a lizard has: just as a gecko makes a copy of its tail, Connors got a copy of an arm and became the Lizard himself. What he needed was a salamander; what he chose was a lizard.

What he needed was a salamander; what he chose was a lizard.

When I pulled that magazine from the bookshelf during that sixth-grade break, I had no idea that the way wounds heal would become the very thing I study. I don’t know where that magazine is now.

But that creature, it turns out, never stayed inside a book. The only Nepali creature with the ability I read about in that story still lives in Maipokhari, Ilam. The thakthake, which still knows how to read the instructions we have forgotten, must surely have come down to the pond again this year after the first monsoon rains to lay its eggs.

title.$t: माईपोखरीको थकथके: काटिएको खुट्टा फेरि पलाउने जीव

content.$t:
भित्तीले पुच्छरको नक्कल बनाउँछ । पूर्वी पहाडको थकथकेले (सालामान्डर) काटिएको खुट्टा हड्डी, नसा र औँलासहित पहिलेकै जस्तो बनाउन सक्छ । त्यही निर्देशन हाम्रो डीएनएमा पनि छ, तर जन्मेपछि त्यसमाथि साँचो लगाइएको छ ।

यो लेख पहिलो पटक २०८३ साउन २६ गते शिलापत्रमा प्रकाशित भएको थियो। मूल लेख पढ्न: https://shilapatra.com/detail/192284

थकथकेले काटिएको खुट्टा कसरी फेरि उमार्छ: एक नजरमा।

सालामान्डरसँग स्कुल बेला भएको मेरो भेट

सालामान्डरसँग मेरो साक्षात्कार सानै बेला भएको थियो । स्कुल बेलैको कुरा हो, कक्षा ६ को जाँचपछि छुट्टीमा घरमा भएको किताबको आल्मारी खोतल्न सुरु गरेँ । त्यही बेला हिन्दीमा लेखिएको पुरानो विज्ञान पत्रिका भेटाएको थिएँ ।

पत्रिकाको नाम याद छैन, कथाको शीर्षक बिर्सिसकेँ, कथाका नायकको नाम पनि भुलिसकेँ । दुर्घटनामा हातखुट्टा गुमाएका एक जना वैज्ञानिकले सालामान्डरको हराएको अंग फेरि उमार्ने क्षमताको प्रयोग आफूमाथि गरेको बारेमा कथा थियो ।  कथाको अन्त्यमा ती जीव वैज्ञानिक सफल भए कि असफल, त्यो पनि सम्झना छैन । तर, सालामान्डरसँग मेरो सम्बन्ध त्यहीँबाट टाँसिएको थियो ।

सालामान्डरको यही अद्भूत क्षमताले ममा जीवविज्ञान पढ्ने हुटहुटी जगेको हो । कथा पढेको धेरैपछिसम्म त सालामान्डरले काटिएका अंग फेरि उमार्नु कथाकारको कल्पना मात्रै ठानेर बसेँ । प्लस टुमा सालामान्डरबारे साँच्चिकै पढेपछि थाहा पाएँ- यिनीहरूमा साँच्चिकै चोट निको पार्ने अद्भूत क्षमता हुन्छ । सालामान्डरको हातखुट्टा, पुच्छर र शरीरका अरु अंग काटियो भने केही महिनामै पहिलेकै जस्तो फर्कन सक्छ ।

कथामा, सालामान्डरमा हुने त्यो क्षमता मान्छेमा सार्नुचाहिँ साँच्चिकै कल्पना मात्रै हो, स्पाइडरम्यानको त्यो लिजार्डवाला खलनायकको जस्तो ।

सालामान्डर र भित्ती एकै होइनन्

मैले स्कुल सक्ने बेलासम्म सालामान्डर भित्तीकै दाजुभाइ हुन् भनेरै बिताएँ- उसको पनि त नयाँ पुच्छर उम्रन्छ । तर, यी दुई दाजुभाइ त परै जाओस्, प्राणीजगत्‌को एउटै वर्गमा पनि नपर्ने रहेछन् ।

भित्ती र छेपारो सरीसृप (Reptile) हुन्- सुक्खा कत्ला भएको छाला, फुल पार्ने, जमिनमै जन्मेर जमिनमै हुर्कने । सालामान्डर भ्यागुताको आफन्त, उभयचर (Amphibian) हो- चिप्लो छाला, पानीमा फुल पार्ने, भुरा पनि चेपागाँडाजस्तै पानीमै हुर्कने ।

सालामान्डर र भित्ती दुवैमा काटिएको पुच्छर उमार्ने बानी भेटिनु एकआपसका आफन्त भएर होइन, दुई फरक बाटोबाट आइपुगेको संयोग हो । अनि, भित्तीले उमार्ने पुच्छर पनि पुरानो पुच्छर होइन, त्यो कुरा पछि आउँछ ।

सालामान्डर अर्थात् माईपोखरीको थकथके

अनि त्यसको निकैपछि मात्रै थाहा पाएको थिएँ- सालामान्डर कुनै टाढा किताबभित्रको जीव मात्र होइन रहेछ । हाम्रै इलामको माईपोखरीमा कति धेरै पाइन्छ । करिब बीस सेन्टिमिटर लामो हुन्छ- खस्रो कालो छाला, त्यसमा सुन्तला रङको दाग । गोहीको जस्तै टाउको र कोखामा हड्डी उठेको हुन्छ । गोहीजस्तै देखिने टाउको र शरीर भएकै कारण थकथकेलाई क्रोकोडाइल न्युट पनि भनिन्छ ।

संसारभरि सालामान्डरका करिब आठ सय प्रजाति छन् । युरोपतिर पाइने र धेरै अध्ययन गरिएको सालामान्डर- न्युट, लगभग हाम्रैजस्तो हुन्छ । तर, अरु धेरै प्रकारका सालामान्डरका प्रजाति छन्- मेक्सिकोमा पाइने एक्सोलोटल जीवनभर बच्चाकै रूपमा बाँच्छ । जापान र चीनका जायन्ट सालामान्डर डेढ मिटरसम्म लामा हुन्छन्- संसारकै सबैभन्दा ठूला उभयचर तिनै हुन् । माईपोखरीको थकथके यी सबैको आफन्त हो, र थकथकेले पनि उही क्षमता बोकेको हुन्छ ।

नेपालको इलाम-पाँचथर, दार्जिलिङ र भुटानवरिपरि पाउने सालामान्डरलाई स्थानीयले थकथके भनेर त चिनिरहेका थिए । तर, बर्मा र चाइनातिर पाइने सालामान्डर (Tylototriton verrucosus) र हाम्रो थकथके एउटै होइनन् भनेर दश वर्षअघि मात्रै थाहा भएको हो ।

सन् २०१४ जुलाईमा जनकराज खतिवडा, शान्ता पौडेल र सुवर्ण घिमिरेले माईपोखरीबाट केही नमुना संकलन गरेका थिए । तिनको शरीरको र डीएनएको बनोट तुलना गर्दा यो त सालामान्डर भएको थाहा पाइएको प्रजाति रहेछ भन्ने पुष्टि भयो । सन् २०१५ मा खतिवडाको टोलीले यसलाई Tylototriton himalayanus नाम दिएर संसारलाई चिनायो ।

माईपोखरीको थकथके इलाम-पाँचथर, दार्जिलिङ र पश्चिम भुटानको करिब नौ सयदेखि दुई हजार छ सय मिटरको उचाइबाहेक संसारमा अन्त कतै भेटिँदैन । नेपालमा भेटिने सालामान्डरको एउटै मात्रै प्रजाति पनि यही नै हो ।

भित्तीले उमारेको पुच्छर उही पुच्छर हो त ?

भित्तीको पुच्छर आफैँ चुँडिँदैन, उसले आफैँ चुँडाउँछ । बिरालोले खेद्‌यो वा कसैले पुच्छर समात्यो भने मांसपेशी खुम्च्याएर आफैँ पुच्छर छोडेर हिँडिदिन्छ । सालामान्डर र भित्तीको फरक यहीँबाट सुरु हुन्छ ।

भित्तीको पुच्छर चुँडिँने ठाउँ जथाभावी हुँदैन । पुच्छरका हड्डीभित्र एउटा कमजोर धर्सो पहिल्यै बनेको हुन्छ । भित्तीको पुच्छर त्यही धर्सोमा मात्रै चुँडिन्छ । रगत बग्ने नसामा पनि बिर्को लगाउन मिल्ने ठाउँहरू हुन्छन् । पुच्छर छुट्टिनेबित्तिकै त्यहाँ बिर्को लाग्छ र रगतको बाटो थुनिदिन्छ, पुच्छर चुँडिँदा रगत बग्दैन ।

छुटेको पुच्छर केही मिनेटसम्म भुईंमा फटफटाइरहन्छ । शरीरबाट छुट्टिएपछि पनि केही समयसम्म त्यसभित्रको नसा र मांसपेशीले काम गरिरहेका हुन्छन् । सिकारीको ध्यान त्यसैले तान्छ, भित्ती उम्किन्छ ।

नयाँ उम्रिएको पुच्छर पहिलेकै पुच्छर होइन, पुच्छरको नक्कल मात्रै हो । पुच्छरभित्रको पुरानो हड्डी फर्किंदैन । हड्डीको सट्टा कार्टिलेजको लामो नली बन्छ । पहिलेजस्तै जोर्नीका गाँठो बन्दैनन्, मेरुदण्डको नसा पूरै फर्किंदैन । बाहिरबाट हेर्दै थाहा हुन्छ- कत्ला फरक रङका हुन्छन्, नयाँ पुच्छर पहिलेभन्दा छोटो पनि हुन्छ । अनि, भित्तीले एकपटक चुँडिएको ठाउँबाट दोस्रोपटक पुच्छर चुँडाउनै सक्दैन । पुच्छर चुँडिने त्यो कमजोर धर्सो हड्डीमा मात्रै हुन्छ । कार्टिलेजको नयाँ नलीमा हुँदैन ।

मैले कथामा पढेको त्यो क्षमता बोकेको एउटै मात्र नेपाली जीव अहिले पनि इलामको माईपोखरीमै छ । हामीले बिर्सिसकेको त्यो निर्देशन अझै पढ्न जान्ने थकथके, बर्खाको पहिलो झरीपछि फुल पार्न पोखरीतिर यसपाली पनि पक्कै झर्‍यो होला ।

भित्तीले पुच्छरजस्तै देखिने अर्को चीज बनाउँछ; सालामान्डरले कोषहरूको पुरानो बनोट नै फर्काउँछ ।

हामीलाई चोट लाग्यो भने के हुन्छ ?

प्रयोगशालामा आएका सामानहरूको कार्टुन खोल्दै गर्दा एक हप्ताअघि पेपर नाइफले अलिकति छोएको थियो । चोर औँलाको नङमाथि लागेको त्यो चोटबाट रगत त केही मिनेटपछि नै बग्न छोड्यो, तर चोटको दाग अझैसम्म छ ।

मेरो औँलामा चोट लाग्दा सबैभन्दा पहिले शरीरले रगत बग्नबाट रोक्न खोज्यो । त्यसपछि प्रतिरक्षा प्रणालीका कोषहरू आएर चोटवरिपरिका फोहोर र किटाणु सफा गर्न थाले । अनि, फाइब्रोब्लास्ट (Fibroblast) कोषहरू घाउ टाल्न कोलाजेनको धागो बुन्न थाले । केही दिनपछि बुनाइ कसिएर घाउ त पुरियो, तर काटेको ठाउँमा दाग बाँकी नै रह्यो ।

हाम्रो शरीरमा घाउ लाग्दा नयाँ बनेको दाग पहिलेको जस्तो छाला बन्न सक्दैन । पुरानो छालामा कोलाजेनको जालो सबै दिशामा मिलेर फैलिएको हुन्छ- माकुराको जालो वा माछा मार्ने जाल बुनेजस्तै । चोट टालिँदा नयाँ कोलाजेन त थपिन्छ, तर तिनको पहिलेजस्तो मिलाइ हुँदैन । हतार-पटारमा चोट पुर्ने चटारोमा कोलाजेन सबैतिर संरचनाबिनै थुप्रिन्छ । चोट टालिएको दागमा रौँ पलाउँदैनन्, पसिना निस्कँदैन, छुँदा छोएको थाहा पनि हुँदैन ।

शरीरले यो बाटो रोज्नुको कारण छ । पहिलेजस्तै छाला फेरि बनाउन हप्तौँ लाग्छ, त्यति नै दिन संक्रमणको खतरा पनि रहन्छ । तैपनि, सालामान्डरजस्तो चोट पुर्ने क्षमता हामीबाट पूरै हराएको छैन । कलेजोको दुईतिहाइ काटेर निकाल्दा पनि बाँकी भाग बढेर केही हप्तामै पहिलेकै तौलमा त पुग्छ, तर पुरानो आकार भने फर्किंदैन । साना बच्चाको औँलाको टुप्पो नङको फेदभन्दा माथिबाट काटियो भने हड्डी, छाला र नङसहित फेरि आउन सक्छ । आमाको गर्भमा सुरुका महिनामा भ्रूणलाई घाउ लाग्यो भने दागबिनै पुरिन्छ ।

हामीमा सालामान्डरजस्तो क्षमता कहिल्यै थिएन भन्ने होइन । हामी हुर्कंदै जाँदा यो क्षमता क्रमशः हराउँदै गयो, सालामान्डरले जीवनभर बचाएर राखिराख्यो ।

एउटा कोषबाट सिङ्गो शरीर

यौनिक प्रजनन् गर्ने हामीजस्ता सबै प्राणीहरूको सुरुवात एउटा कोषबाट भएको हुन्छ । त्यो कोष दुई हुन्छ, दुईबाट चार, चारबाट आठ । केही दिनमै कोषको सानो डल्लो बन्छ- मोरुला (Morula) । यतिबेलासम्म सबै कोष उस्तै हुन्छन् । कसैलाई आफूले पछि के बन्ने हो भन्ने थाहा भइसकेको हुँदैन, सबै सबै थोक बन्न सक्छन् ।

मोरुलामा थप विभाजन सुरु भएपछि सुरुमा ब्लास्टुला (Blastula) बन्छ । कोषहरू अब के बन्ने भनेर छान्न सुरु गर्छन् । भ्रूणको आकार बढ्दै गर्दा तीनवटा पत्र छुट्टिन्छन् । सबैभन्दा बाहिरी पत्र छाला र स्नायु बन्छ । बीचको पत्र हड्डी, मांसपेशी, मुटु र रगत । भित्री पत्रबाट आन्द्रा, फोक्सो र कलेजो । हातखुट्टा बनाउने कोषहरू बीचको पत्रबाट आउँछन् ।

प्राय: जीवहरूमा कोषहरू के बन्ने भनेर एकपटक छानेपछि फर्कन पाउँदैनन्; मुटुको कोष बनिसकेपछि त्यो फेरि छालाको कोष बन्न सक्दैन ।

सालामान्डरले कसरी नयाँ हातखुट्टा फेरि उमार्छ ?

हाम्रो शरीरमा चोट लाग्यो भने शरीरलाई जतिसक्दो कोलाजेन बनाएर घाउ टाल्ने चटारो हुन्छ, सालामान्डरमा त्यसको ठ्याक्कै उल्टो ।

सालामान्डरको खुट्टा काटियो भने पहिलो केही मिनेटमै छेउबाट छालाका कोषहरू सर्दै आउँछन् । बाह्र घन्टाभित्रै घाउमाथि पातलो पत्र बनिसक्छ । हामीलाई जस्तो रगत जमेर पाप्रा बस्दैन, सुरुदेखि नै छालाजस्तै कोषहरूले छोपिन्छ । काटिएको ठाउँमा नयाँ बनेका कोषहरूले भित्रको सतहमा भएका फाइब्रोब्लास्टमा रसायन पठाइरहन्छन् । मान्छेमा जस्तै कोलाजेनको भताभुङ्ग जालो थुपारेर हतारमा चोट लागेको ठाउँ टाल्ने चटारो सुरु नै हुन पाउँदैन ।

अझै अचम्मको परिवर्तन त चोट लागेको ठाउँ वरिपरिका कोषहरूमा हुन्छ । नजिकका मांसपेशी, हड्डी र कार्टिलेजले आफ्नो पहिचान छोडिदिन्छन् । म मांसपेशी हुँ भन्ने बिर्सन्छन्, र फेरि भ्रूणको अवस्थाका कोषजस्तै बन्छन् । चोट लागेको ठाउँमा त्यसपछि कोषहरू थुप्रिएर सानो डल्लो बन्छ- ब्लास्टेमा (Blastema)। भ्रूण विकाश हुने बेला मात्रै तीन पत्र छुट्टिएपछि फेरि फर्कन नपाउने स्थापित भएको नियमलाई सालामान्डरले यहीँ तोडेको हुन्छ ।

सालामान्डरमा ब्लास्टेमा बन्नका लागि रगतको नसा चाहिन्छ, प्रतिरक्षा प्रणालीका कोषहरू नभए घाउ निको बनाउने प्रयास सुरु नै हुन सक्दैन । रगतका नसालले सालामान्डरलाई चोट लागेपछि पनि पहिलेकै जस्तै रसायनहरू पुर्‍याइरहन्छ । यही रसायनहरूले चोट लागेको ठाउँमा नयाँ बनेका ब्लास्टेमाका कोषलाई बाँडिइरहन अह्राउँछन् ।

सालामान्डरको हातखुट्टा सँगै नसा पनि काटियो भने यो सबै प्रक्रिया सुरु नै हुन पाउँदैन । ब्लास्टेमा बनेका सबै कोषले सबथोक बनाउन सक्छन् भन्नेचाहिँ हुँदैन- पुराना कोषहरू फेरिएर पहिलेकै काम पहिलेकै ठाउँमा गर्न दोहोर्‍याउन सक्ने मात्रै हुन्छन् । मांसपेशीबाट आएको कोष फेरि मांसपेशी नै बन्छ, कार्टिलेजबाट आएको कार्टिलेज । छाला छाला नै बन्छ, नसा नसा नै ।

ब्लास्टेमाको डल्लो ठूलो हुँदै गएपछि भ्रूण बेलामा छाडेको कामहरू फेरि दोहोरिन्छ । खुट्टा बनाउने जिनहरू ब्लास्टेमा फेरि खुल्न सुरु गर्छन् । सालामान्डरले नयाँ तरिका पत्ता लगाएको होइन, आफ्नै पुरानो निर्देशन पहिलेजस्तै फेरि पढ्न सुरु गरेको हो । भ्रूण अवस्थामा जस्रै कोषहरू फेरि बाँडिन्छन्- कोही हड्डी बन्छन्, कोही मांसपेशी, कोही नसा, कोही छाला ।

सालामान्डरले नयाँ तरिका पत्ता लगाएको होइन, आफ्नै पुरानो निर्देशन पहिलेजस्तै फेरि पढ्न सुरु गरेको हो ।

अनि, यी कोषलाई आफू खुट्टाको कुन ठाउँमा छु भन्ने पनि थाहा हुन्छ । भ्रूणमा खुट्टा बन्दा हरेक कोषले आफ्नो ठेगाना बोकेको हुन्छ- म काँधबाट कति टाढा छु भन्ने । हुर्केपछि पनि त्यो ठेगाना मेटिँदैन । ब्लास्टेमासँग बन्नुपर्ने खुट्टाको तस्वीर हुँदैन, ठेगाना मात्रै हुन्छ । काटिएको ठाउँका कोषले आफ्नो ठेगाना पढ्छन्, अनि त्योभन्दा तलको जति बाँकी छ त्यति बनाउँछन् । त्यसैले नाडीबाट काटियो भने पन्जा मात्रै बन्छ, काँधबाट काटियो भने काँधदेखि तलको पूरै खुट्टा ।

सालामान्डरलाई नयाँ खुट्टा उम्रन एक-दुई महिना लाग्छ । ठूलो सालामान्डरलाई झन् बढी । नयाँ बनेको खुट्टा सुरुमा पहिलेभन्दा सानो हुन्छ, अनि बिस्तारै बढेर पुरानै आकारको हुन्छ । नयाँ खुट्टा भित्तीको पुच्छरजस्तो नक्कल होइन- हड्डी हड्डीकै ठाउँमा, जोर्नी जोर्नीकै ठाउँमा, औँला उति नै संख्यामा पहिलेजस्तै बन्छ ।

तर, सालामान्डरको यो क्षमताको पनि सीमा हुन्छ। काटिएको ठाउँबाट बाहिरतिर मात्रै नयाँ बन्छ । खुट्टा बन्छ, पुच्छर बन्छ, बङ्गारा बन्छ । एउटै ठाउँबाट पटक-पटक काटिँदै गयो भने नयाँ खुट्टा बिस्तारै पहिलेजस्तो बन्न सक्दैन- औँला कम हुन्छन्, कहिले बाङ्गो हुन्छ । टाउको या मुटुमा चोट लाग्यो भने ठीक पार्न सक्छन्, तर टाउको वा शरीर काटियो भने यिनीहरू पनि मर्छन् ।

हाम्रो शरीर सालामान्डरजस्तो चोट निको पार्न सक्ने किन भएन त ?

हाम्रो शरीरमा तातो रगत हुन्छ, त्यही न्यानोमा ब्याक्टेरिया छिटो बढ्छ । त्यसैले घाउ जति समय खुला राख्यो, जोखिम उति नै बढी । हाम्रो प्रतिरक्षा प्रणाली त्यही हिसाबले बनेको हुन्छ- चोट लाग्नेबित्तिकै सुजन (Inflammation) हुन्छ, त्यसले न्युट्रोफिल र म्याक्रोफेज कोषहरूलाई बोलाउँछ, अनि तिनकै सङ्केत पाएर फाइब्रोब्लास्टले चटारोमा घाउ टाल्न सुरु गर्छ ।

सालामान्डरको रगत चिसो हुन्छ, चिसो पानीमा बस्छ । त्यहाँ ब्याक्टेरिया हाम्रो शरीरमा जति छिटो बढ्न सक्दैनन्, र घाउ केही हप्ता खुला राख्दा पनि त्यति ठूलो जोखिम हुँदैन । सालामान्डरलाई चोट लाग्दा पनि सुरुमा म्याक्रोफेज आउँछन्, तर तिनको हतार घाउ पुर्नेभन्दा पनि सुजन साम्य पार्ने रसायन चुहाउनेतिर हुन्छ । चोट लागेको ठाउँ शान्त रहन्छ र त्यही शान्तिमा ब्लास्टेमा बनेर घाउ पुरिन थाल्छ । प्रयोगशालामा म्याक्रोफेज हटाइदियो भने सालामान्डरमा पनि हाम्रो जस्तै दाग बस्छ ।

बन्द गरिएको त्यो साँचो कहाँ छ ?

सालामान्डरलाई चोट निको पार्ने चाहिने जिनहरू हामीसँग पनि छन् । ब्लास्टेमामा खुलेका जिनहरू सालामान्डरले नयाँ बनाएको होइन । हामी भ्रूणमा हुँदा हाम्रो हात बनाउने बेला तिनै जिनले काम गरेका थिए । हाम्रो शरीरको विकास हुँदै जाँदा ती बिस्तारै बन्द भएका मात्रै हुन् ।

हाम्रो शरीरका हरेक कोषमा उही डीएनए हुन्छ । छालाको कोषमा पनि मुटु बनाउने जिन हुन्छ, मुटुको कोषमा पनि छाला बनाउने । फरक कुन जिन बोकेको छ भन्नेमा होइन, कुन खुला छ र कुन बन्द छ भन्नेमा हुन्छ ।

जिनहरू बन्द गर्ने काम क्रोमोजोमको डीएनएमाथि लगाइने रासायनिक चिनोले गर्छ । मिथाइल (Methyl) को सानो अणु क्रोमोजोममा टाँसिएको आधारमा कुन जिन बन्द र कुन खुला भन्ने थाहा हुन्छ । मिथाइल धेरै भएको भागको डीएनए हिस्टोन (Histone) भनिने प्रोटिनको फिर्कोमा कस्सिएर बेरिएको हुन्छ, जिन पढ्ने मेसिन त्यहाँ पुग्नै पाउँदैन । क्रोमोजोममा मिथाइलका अणुहरू थोरै जोडिएर खुला भएको ठाउँको जिनबाट मात्रै आरएनए र प्रोटिन बन्न सक्छ ।

हामीमा, एकपटक शरीर बनिसकेपछि भ्रूणबेलाका जिनहरू त्यसैगरी बन्द गरिएका हुन्छन् । मिथाइलको चिनो लाग्छ, डीएनए कस्सिएर बेरिन्छ, अनि कोषले आफ्नो काम मात्रै गर्न थाल्छ । जिनहरू एकपटक बन्द भएपछि, त्यो चिनोसहित कोषविभाजन भएर अर्को कोषमा सर्दै जान्छ- छाला छालै बन्छ, मुटु मुटु नै ।

हामीमा जिनहरूलाई लगाएको यही भोटे ताल्चा चोट लागेको बेला खुल्दैन । हाम्रो घाउमा पनि जिन खुल्छन्, तर ती कोलाजेन बनाउने जिन हुन्, हात बनाउने होइनन् ।

सालामान्डरमा यही चिनो चोट लागेपछि खुल्छ । घाउका कोषमा मिथाइल हटाउने प्रोटिन सक्रिय हुन्छ, कस्सिएको डीएनए खुल्न थाल्छ, अनि भ्रूण बन्द भएका बेला जिन फेरि पढिन थाल्छन् । कोषले आफ्नो पहिचान छोड्नु भनेको यही हो- डीएनए फेरिएको होइन, त्यसमाथिको ताल्चा खुलेको हो ।

डीएनए फेरिएको होइन, त्यसमाथिको ताल्चा खुलेको हो ।

डीएनए दुवैमा उही हो; फरक कुन भाग पढ्न पाइन्छ भन्नेमा छ । यही ताल्चाको कुरा गर्दा सालामान्डरको जिनोम पनि हेर्नुपर्ने हुन्छ ।

सालामान्डरको डीएनए हाम्रोभन्दा दस गुणा ठूलो हुन्छ । हामीमा तीन अर्ब न्युक्लियोटाइड छन्, मेक्सीकोको सालामान्डर, एक्सोलोटलमा बत्तीस अर्ब । क्रोमोजोमको संख्या भने हाम्रोभन्दा कम- हाम्रोमा ४६, उनीहरूको २८ । एक्सोलोटलका २८ क्रोमोजोम हाम्रोभन्दा धेरै ठूला हुन्छन्, तर जिनको संख्या हाम्रैजस्तै । थपिएका सबै डीएनए जिन-जिनको बीचमा हुन्छ, दोहोरिने अक्षरका लामा टुक्रा भएर बसेको हुन्छन् । कुन जिन कहिले खोल्ने भन्ने निर्णय गर्ने र नियन्त्रण जिनहरूबीचमा भएका डीएनएले गेरेका हुन्  ।

एक्सोलोटलको जिनोम हाम्रोभन्दा दश गुणा ठूलो छ, तर जिनको संख्या उति नै हो । तर, यत्रो डीएनए बोकेर पनि सालामान्डरसँग हामीसँग नभएको कुनै जादुको जिन छैन । फरक यति हो, ठूलो जिनोम बोक्दा कोष ठूलो हुनुपर्छ, अनि कोष ठूलो भएपछि विभाजन ढिलो हुन्छ । सालामान्डरलाई नयाँ खुट्टा उमार्न महिनौँ लाग्नुको एउटा कारण यही हो ।

सालामान्डरमा कोष विभाजन कम हुने भएर, उनीहरूमा क्यान्सरको खतरा तुलनात्मक रूपमा कम हुन्छ । त्यसैले, सालामान्डरले जिनहरूलाई साँचो नलगाई राख्न सक्छन्, हाम्रोमा क्यान्सरको खतरा टाल्न ताल्चा लगाइएको हुन्छ । ब्लास्टेमामा खुल्ने जिन दुवैसँग छन्, फरक त ती कहिले खुल्छन् र कहिले बन्द हुन्छन् भन्नेमा छ ।

अनि, अहिले वैज्ञानिकहरू के गरिरहेका छन् त ?

एक्सोलोटलको पूरै जिनोम सन् २०१८ मा मात्रै पढेर सकियो । त्यसपछि ब्लास्टेमाका कोषले आफ्नो ठेगाना कसरी सम्झन्छन् भन्ने थाहा भयो- काँधतिरका कोषमा एउटा प्रोटिन बाक्लो हुँदो रहेछ, औँलातिरकामा पातलो। प्रयोगशालामा त्यो प्रोटिन बढाइदियो भने पन्जा मात्रै उमार्न लागेको ब्लास्टेमाले पूरै पाखुरा उमार्न थाल्छ ।

सालामान्डरको क्षमताको प्रयोग मुसामाथि पनि भइरहेको छ । औँलाको टुप्पो काटेर त्यहाँ सालामान्डरको जस्तै प्रोटिन बढाइदियो भने दाग बस्नुको साटो हड्डी र नङसहित केही भाग फेरि आएको छ ।

तर, मानिसमा सालामान्डरको क्षमता सार्ने सम्भावनाबारे हामी अड्किएर सोच्नुपर्छ । जुन सुजन रोकेर दाग हटाइन्छ, त्यसैले संक्रमण पनि रोकिरहेको हुन्छ । जुन ताल्चा खोलेर कोषलाई पहिचान छाड्न लगाइन्छ, त्यही ताल्चा खुला रह्यो भने कोष जथाभावी बाँडिएर क्यान्सर बन्न थाल्छ ।

त्यसैले अहिलेको काम पूरै हात उमार्नेतिर छैन । डाइबिटिजका बिरामीको ननिको हुने घाउ दागबिनै पुर्ने, जलेको छालामा पसिना ग्रन्थी फर्काउने, हृदयघात हुँदा मुटुमा बनेको दागलाई मांसपेशीमा बदल्ने- यस्तै स-साना काम भइरहेका छन् ।

अनि, त्यो कथा

आज मैले त्यो कथा फेरि सम्झिँदा, स्पाइडरमेन कमिक्सको कथालाई हिन्दीमा लेखेको हो जस्तो लाग्छ । स्पाइडरम्यानका डा. कर्ट कोनर्सले खोजेको पनि यही थियो । दुर्घटनामा एउटा हात गुमाएका उनले छेपाराको जिन आफूमाथि प्रयोग गरे । हात त पलायो । तर, छेपाराको जिनले छेपाराले जति नै दिन्छ- भित्तीले पुच्छरको नक्कल बनाएझैँ कोनर्सले हातको नक्कल पाए, अनि आफैँ लिजार्ड बने । उनलाई चाहिएको सालामान्डर थियो, रोजेको छेपारो ।

उनलाई चाहिएको सालामान्डर थियो, रोजेको छेपारो ।

कक्षा ६ को त्यो छुट्टीमा आल्मारीबाट पत्रिका झिक्दा मलाई थाहा थिएन, चोट कसरी निको हुन्छ भन्ने कुरा नै पढ्ने विषय बनाएर बस्नेछु भनेर । त्यो पत्रिका अब कहाँ छ, थाहा छैन ।

तर, त्यो जीव भने किताबभित्रकै रहेनछ । मैले कथामा पढेको त्यो क्षमता बोकेको एउटै मात्र नेपाली जीव अहिले पनि इलामको माईपोखरीमै छ । हामीले बिर्सिसकेको त्यो निर्देशन अझै पढ्न जान्ने थकथके, बर्खाको पहिलो झरीपछि फुल पार्न पोखरीतिर यसपाली पनि पक्कै झर्‍यो होला ।

यो पनि पढ्नुहोस्

  • हात्तीलाई मानिसझैँ क्यान्सर किन लाग्दैन?

title.$t: Lobsters Don’t Age: Telomerase, Telomeres and the Price of Living Forever

content.$t:
The Trade-Off Multicellular Life Makes with Death

Lobsters don’t grow old. An enzyme called telomerase keeps their cells young for a century or more, yet every lobster still dies. Starting from an empty crab shell on a rice-field ridge in Jhapa, this essay follows the…

*A lobster that has grown for 100 years and one that has just turned 10 have telomeres of the same length on their chromosomes. Shortening telomeres are the primary clock driving us toward old age; in the lobster, that clock simply doesn’t exist.*

This article was first published in Nepali on Onlinekhabar in August 2026 (Bhadau 2, 2083 BS). This is the author’s own English translation. Read the original: onlinekhabar.com ↗

Why lobsters don’t grow old, but still die, at a glance.

The empty crab shell you find on the ridge of a rice field is merely the old shell a crab outgrew and left behind; the crab itself hasn’t died. The lobster, the crab’s sea-dwelling relative with the same shell-shedding habit, never grows old. The enzyme telomerase renders a lobster’s cells immortal, but our own bodies keep that very enzyme under lock and key.

The Empty Crab Shell on the Field’s Edge

My school summer holidays were spent playing in the mud of monsoon rice fields. I was always afraid of running into a crab out there. They built their homes in the ridges between the fields, and the water leaking through their holes drove everyone mad. Sometimes, on those ridges, I would find a crab-shaped shell: two pincers (claws), eight legs, even the little sockets for the eyes, all exactly in place, but completely empty inside. Even finding one thrilled me that a crab had died.

Only long after I left school did I learn that the “dead crab” I had found was just the old shell a crab had outgrown and abandoned. A crab has no bones; its outer shell is its skeleton. As a crab grows, its body gets bigger, but its shell stays the same size. Once its body has grown, the crab splits the old shell open from behind and climbs out, building a new shell again and again throughout its life.

The crab that left its shell on that ridge in Jhapa had simply shed its old shell, and the crab itself was hiding in a burrow a little way off, waiting for its new shell to harden.

The crab has many relatives that share the habit of shedding their shells. Its giant cousin lives in the sea: the lobster. The design is the same: an outer shell, ten legs, and two large claws in front. The only differences are that the lobster lives in salt water, grows much larger, and lives far longer than a crab.

Four Hundred Years Ago, Lobsters Were Gathered by the Bucket

Four hundred years ago, lobsters were everywhere around New England (Boston) in North America. According to European settlers’ accounts, every morning the waves left “piles of lobsters two feet high” on the shore. You could take a bucket and gather as many as you liked. But not to eat or sell: farmers used lobsters to fertilize their fields.

Found everywhere in the sea, the lobster was called the cockroach of the sea. The name wasn’t given for nothing; it was food for the poor, servants, and prisoners. In the eighteenth century, prisoners in America are even said to have protested against lobster being served more than three times a week. It sounds astonishing today, but back then nobody liked lobster.

Today, a plate of lobster costs nearly 100 dollars, and we consider it a luxury. In the very New England waters where lobsters teemed three or four hundred years ago, they are now disappearing. Overfishing is one reason, of course, but the warming sea is shrinking their numbers every year.

In warm water, their shells are more susceptible to disease, and the young struggle to grow. As a result, New England’s lobsters are slowly being pushed north in search of colder water.

The Creature That Never Grows Old

So far, the lobster’s story sounds as ordinary as any other creature’s: the sea warmed, so they moved north in search of colder water.

Lobster numbers in the sea fall every year. But here is the most astonishing part: almost all creatures grow old and die of old age. This is exactly where the lobster is different: if nature has made any creature immortal, it is the lobster.

The secret of the lobster’s immortality lies in telomerase. Our bodies have telomerase too, but they keep it locked away.

The crabs I found on those ridges grow old and die; their life cycle is limited. But a lobster never grows old; it shows no signs of aging. If you pulled a hundred-year-old lobster and a ten-year-old lobster out of the sea and examined them, you would find no real difference at the genetic level. Its body grows bigger with age, but its muscles stay just as strong. Its ability to lay eggs does not decline with age; instead, it increases as the body grows larger. And it is not only the muscles: the ability of its cells to divide remains the same in lobsters of every age.

In other words, whatever cells, muscle, and physical capacity a young lobster has, it retains them a hundred years later. For us humans, after age thirty, the chance of dying from biological causes doubles every eight years; for a lobster, that chance stays the same no matter how old it gets. If lobsters could keep shedding their shells, they could live forever. But even though their cells never age, once their bodies have grown very large, lobsters stop making new shells.

The oldest lobsters we have found so far are only about 140–150 years old. This raises the question: if lobsters can truly live forever, why do they die?

To Be Multicellular Is to Accept Death

To find the answer, we have to set the lobster aside for a moment and go far back in time, to when there was only single-celled life on Earth.

There is a bacterium in pond water. It has enough food, and the temperature is right. It stretches its body, copies its DNA, and splits down the middle into two. There is no way to tell which is the mother and which the offspring; both are the same, both are new. Bacteria die of hunger, heat, poison, or being killed by other creatures. But a bacterium never dies of old age; aging simply does not exist in its life.

For roughly the first three billion years, life on Earth carried on just like this: there was death, but no aging. Only about a billion years ago did single-celled organisms begin to become multicellular. Instead of separating after cell division, some cells began to stick together and divide the work: some became the outer layer, some digested food, and some provided movement.

A single-celled organism, given the right conditions, can keep dividing and live forever. But when trillions of cells come together to form a heart, a brain, and a body, they must be disciplined: divide only when needed, repair their own damage, and if they can’t repair it, remove themselves for the good of the body.

So cells stopped seeking the kind of immortality bacteria have and began to share the work instead. The job of carrying on the lineage was taken by a select few cells, called ‘germ cells’ (reproductive cells). The body’s immune system needs new cells, and there is a small reserve to supply them: ‘stem cells.’ All the rest, in the heart, the skin, the liver, became the ‘somatic cells’ (ordinary body cells) that keep the body running. As we age, every somatic cell’s ability to copy itself declines. The struggle to replace the body’s worn-out cells grows with age, and that is what we call aging.

Where Is a Cell’s Age Written?

We have all seen the small plastic tips on both ends of a shoelace. Those little plastic tips do nothing for the lace itself; they don’t make it stronger or longer. They are there to stop the lace from fraying at its ends, and they wear away the older the shoe gets. Just by looking at those plastic tips, anyone can easily guess how many times the shoe has been worn.

Like a shoelace, each chromosome has a record at both ends of how many times a cell can divide or has already divided. At each end of every chromosome, there is a repeating sequence of nucleotides, TTAGGG, TTAGGG (in lobsters, TTAGG, TTAGG), repeated thousands of times. This structure, called the telomere, makes no protein and carries no trait for the body. It works like the plastic tip of a shoelace, protecting the useful DNA inside from fraying.

Every time a cell divides, a new copy of each chromosome must be made. Copying chromosomes is the job of an enzyme called DNA polymerase, and this is where the trouble begins. DNA polymerase cannot reach the very tip of the chromosome and copy it exactly. As a result, every time a cell divides, the telomere loses a few dozen nucleotides.

Just as the plastic on a shoelace wears away a little each time you put the shoe on, each new cell division shortens the telomere. At first, this does no harm. But there is a limit to how short it can get before it matters. In humans, somatic cells divide about 50 times on average. After that, the shortened telomere can no longer protect the chromosome’s structure. Scientists call this limit, beyond which the telomere is too short to keep the chromosome intact, the Hayflick limit.

Once the telomere passes this limit, the chromosome’s structure begins to break down. Inside the cell, a kind of guard patrols: the ATM and ATR kinases. They recognize chromosomes with shortened telomeres as broken DNA. Their message reaches p53, the strongest guard keeping watch inside the cell. Once alerted, p53 orders the cell to stop dividing. Cells that can no longer divide are called ‘senescent cells’ (worn-out cells).

Senescent cells do not die, but they also cannot divide again. Though they can no longer be replaced by new cells, they do not sit quietly. They continue to leak molecules that drive ‘inflammation’ (swelling) and enzymes that break down the surrounding tissue.

Until we are about 20–25 years old, senescent cells make little difference to the body. In fact, they alert the immune system so that wounds heal quickly. But as we age, the immune system can no longer clear them away properly everywhere. Their numbers pile up, and the body lives with constant inflammation. This is what we understand as a body gripped by aging.

Like the plastic tip of a shoelace, the telomere at the end of each chromosome gets shorter with every cell division.

The Secret of the Lobster That Never Ages: The Telomerase Enzyme

Lobster cells have an enzyme that is always at work: telomerase. Every time a cell divides, it keeps the telomeres at the ends of the chromosomes from getting shorter. Its job is to add back the telomere letters lost in each division. In a lobster’s somatic cells, telomerase is always active. However, even when the body’s cells are replaced many times, the tips of the chromosomes stay the same.

The secret of the lobster’s immortality lies in telomerase. Our bodies have telomerase too, just like the lobster’s. But the body keeps it locked away. In all our somatic cells, except germ cells, stem cells, and some immune cells, the gene that produces telomerase is permanently switched off.

Lobsters still die, and the reason is not an aging body but their inability to make a new shell.

That is why, in the cells of our skin, liver, and muscles, once telomeres start to shorten, they can never grow long again, just as the plastic tip of a shoelace can never return to its original state once it starts to fray. In lobster cells, it is the opposite. Take cells from any organ, such as muscle, liver, nerve, or ovary, and telomerase is switched on.

The result is simple: no matter how many times the cells divide, the tips of the chromosomes remain unchanged. The telomeres never reach the Hayflick limit, the ATM and ATR kinases never receive a signal of DNA damage, p53 is never activated, and the cells never have to become senescent, or old.

A lobster that has grown for 100 years and one that has just turned 10 have telomeres of the same length on their chromosomes. Shortening telomeres are the primary clock driving us toward old age; in the lobster, that clock simply doesn’t exist.

Why Did Our Bodies Lock Telomerase Away?

So why is the telomerase that runs nonstop in lobsters switched off in us? Why not just unlock it? If our somatic cells could keep their telomeres long forever, it seems we would never age. Why didn’t nature make us like lobsters?

In fact, this very option is being tested inside our bodies every day. The name of that experiment is cancer.

Cancer is not an enemy from outside. It is our own somatic cells breaking the bargain struck a billion years ago and trying to return to the old, single-celled way of life. Ignoring signals from neighboring cells, disregarding warnings that DNA is damaged, and racing to make copies of themselves: all of this comes naturally to bacteria. But inside a body made of trillions of cells, the same behavior becomes deadly.

Even cells trying to become bacteria-like in this way cannot divide more than about fifty times; the same Hayflick limit stops them, too. That is why; to become cancerous, cells must first stop their telomeres from shortening. That is exactly what we find in about 90 percent of cancers: the lock on telomerase has been opened. First, mutations pile up, and by the time the cancer has formed, the chains holding back the TERT gene, which makes telomerase, have come loose, and the tumor spreads unchecked.

Like lobster cells, cancer is immortal too. In 1951, Henrietta Lacks was 31 when she arrived at a hospital in Baltimore with cervical cancer. During her treatment, a small piece of her tumor was taken and sent to the lab for cell culture. Henrietta died that same year, but her tumor did not. It kept dividing and dividing. The “HeLa cells” taken from her tumor are still alive in laboratories seventy years later.

So Why Didn’t the Lobster Become a Cancer Factory?

An obvious question may arise here: if telomerase is always active in lobsters, shouldn’t they be cancer factories? Yet it is fair to say that cancer has not been found in lobsters; so far, evidence of tumors in them is negligible.

We can guess at a few reasons. First, telomerase alone is not enough to cause cancer. Telomerase is only one key; for cancer to form, many other systems have to be disrupted one after another.

In our bodies, telomere length is just one wall among many. The lobster lacking that one wall does not mean all the other walls have fallen. Even though telomerase keeps working and the lobster’s telomeres never shorten, other safeguards that prevent cancer are still on duty.

Not aging is not the same as being immortal. For lobster or human, death is inevitable for every multicellular creature.

Second, a lobster’s body has few organs that, like ours, must divide every day. The cells of our gut, skin and blood have to be renewed daily. The more cells divide, the more chances there are for mutations. And cancer, too, usually starts in exactly such fast-dividing places.

By producing telomerase, lobsters switch off the clock that marks the body’s age. Their telomeres don’t shorten, and they don’t get cancer the way we do. Lobsters still die, but not because of an aging body. The reason is their ability to make a new shell.

And One Day, the Lobster Stops Molting

Just like a crab’s, a lobster’s outer shell is its skeleton, and it does not grow. To grow bigger, it has to molt. But the bigger the body gets, the thicker and heavier the new shell has to be. The energy and calcium this requires rise many times over as the body grows. A lobster that molts two or three times a year when small can manage only once every two or three years once it is big.

Molting is risky in itself. To escape its old shell, a lobster must pull its ten legs, two large claws, and the rest of its body through a single narrow opening. This is especially difficult for large lobsters; some die of exhaustion with the old shell half split and half their body still inside.

The longer it lives, the more energy each molt costs. As age and body size increase, gathering the energy to molt becomes harder and harder. One day it is simply exhausted, stops molting, and stays in its old shell. Once it stops molting, the trouble only grows: bacterial disease in the old shell slowly reaches the body, and that infection takes its life.

Other Creatures That Don’t Age Like the Lobster

There are many other creatures as strange as the lobster. Pond water is home to a small invertebrate called the hydra. About a centimeter long, the hydra does not age: its body is made of ‘stem cells’ and can keep replacing them as needed. In the Mediterranean lives a jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii. It goes one step beyond the lobster or the hydra: when it is starved or injured, it returns to its juvenile stage and starts its life cycle over again.

The salamander, which drew me to biology as a child, is found in our own part of the world. Cut off a leg, and it grows a new one, complete with bone, muscle, nerves, and skin. Even a lizard can grow a new tail, but a salamander can rebuild the lens of its eye, part of its heart, and even its head. Salamanders can activate both telomerase and stem cells, yet they are not immortal either. However well they can repair a broken body, they are not immortal.

In the end, the hydra escaped aging by keeping its body simple. The jellyfish turned back the clock. The salamander retained the power to repair what breaks. The lobster left the telomerase lock open. Four different paths, yet all their bodies eventually wear out. They die of everything except old age.

The shell I found in that field in Jhapa was not a crab’s skeleton. But somewhere on the seafloor, a lobster lies waiting to die in a half-split shell. This is what the lobster’s story teaches: not aging is not the same as being immortal. For every multicellular creature, lobster or human, death is inevitable.

title.$t: COVID-19, Long COVID and the Old Diseases It Reawakens

content.$t:
Your PCR test is negative, so why are you still exhausted? A new review suggests COVID may wake up viruses and TB that have been hiding in your body for years.

Once the virus has vanished from the body, or the PCR report has come back negative for COVID-19, why doesn’t the body signal that the war is over?

This article was first published in Nepali on Ukaalo on December 26, 2025 (Poush 11, 2082 BS). This is the author’s own English translation. Read the original: ukaalo.com ↗

There have been studies on what the coronavirus (COVID-19) is and how it spreads, but much remains to be studied about the changes the body undergoes after a COVID-19 infection and about how long COVID develops. In this context, a paper published by Rutgers Medical College has raised a question and a suspicion: could the long-term effects seen after COVID-19 be caused not by COVID-19 alone, but by our own body’s hidden enemies that rise up during the infection?

COVID-19 and Its Link to SARS

Beginning in the Chinese city of Wuhan toward the end of 2019, the COVID-19 infection spread within a few months into a worldwide pandemic. First identified five years ago, COVID-19 has affected most of the world’s people directly or indirectly. COVID-19 was given the name ‘SARS-CoV-2.’ It is a respiratory virus, meaning it affects the respiratory system.

The virus that causes COVID-19 is called SARS-CoV-2 because of the SARS epidemic in China in 2002–03. COVID-19 and SARS are both respiratory diseases, and their effects are similar. SARS-CoV-2, the virus behind COVID-19, is structurally and genetically similar to SARS-CoV-1, the virus that causes SARS.

Unlike SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV-1 did not attach easily to human cells. Because researchers identified infections quickly, the epidemic did not spread worldwide. The SARS outbreak at that time was limited to about ten thousand infections, and nearly a thousand people died of it.

SARS-CoV-2 carries spike proteins on its outer surface that can easily attach to cells in our respiratory tract. Because of this ability, COVID-19 spreads more easily than SARS, and an infected person can quickly pass it on to others. That is why COVID-19 spread to every continent in such a short time.

Questions About COVID’s Long-Term Effects

In most people, a COVID infection lasts two to three weeks. Once COVID has healed, the body has cleared SARS-CoV-2. Even though our immune system has removed the virus, that doesn’t mean the infection’s effects are over. In some people, various problems continue for months afterward. These long-term effects of COVID-19 are what we call long COVID.

SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, cannot hide in our bodies. If the virus itself is no longer present, how do its long-term effects persist? Scientists are investigating this very question. In this context, a study recently published by researchers at Rutgers University has raised an important question: could long COVID be caused by COVID-19 reactivating other infections that were already hiding in the body?

The Structure of SARS-CoV-2 and How It Enters the Body

For most of us, COVID-19 begins when SARS-CoV-2 infects cells in the respiratory system. The virus can enter the body through the nose, mouth, or eyes via tiny droplets (aerosols) released when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or speaks.

Once inside the body, the virus’s first target is the cells of the lungs and respiratory system, whose surfaces carry a protein called the ACE2 receptor. Normally, the ACE2 receptor helps cells with external signaling and biological regulation. But in COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2 uses this very ACE2 receptor as its main entry point into the cell.

SARS-CoV-2 is an RNA virus. Just as we keep our genetic information in the DNA of our chromosomes, some viruses store it in RNA. SARS-CoV-2 has no DNA and has no need for it. Its genome is positive-sense RNA at the virus’s core. Being positive sense means that once it enters a host cell, it can readily use the cell’s machinery to make viral proteins. At the start of infection, SARS-CoV-2 does not need to enter the host cell’s nucleus or make new DNA or extra RNA first.

The outside of SARS-CoV-2 is covered by a lipid viral envelope that protects the virus. Soap and water, alcohol, or hand sanitizer can kill the virus by disrupting this envelope. Inside the viral envelope, the membrane contains three types of protein: spike, membrane, and envelope proteins. Of these, the membrane and envelope proteins provide the virus’s structural protection. At the virus’s core is its RNA, wrapped and protected by the nucleocapsid protein.

The Spike Protein and the Start of Infection

Spike proteins are the most important part of SARS-CoV-2 infection. They are also why COVID-19 is called a coronavirus. They look like a crown (corona in Latin) on the virus’s outer surface and come in two types: spike-1 and spike-2. Spike-1 attaches to the host cell’s ACE2 receptor, while spike-2 helps fuse the virus and host cell membranes. Compared with SARS-CoV-1, the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 binds to the host cell’s ACE2 receptor much more easily and strongly. This is why COVID-19 spread across the world much more easily and quickly than SARS.

Once the virus’s spike protein binds to the host cell’s ACE2 receptor, a cell protease called TMPRSS2 becomes active. Able to cut proteins like scissors, it snips part of the spike protein, triggering the virus’s entry and opening the way for the viral RNA to enter the host cell.

In some cases, when TMPRSS2 is scarce, or the virus has mutated, the viral RNA can also enter the host cell through a process called endocytosis. The virus and the ACE2 receptor together form a small, spherical structure called an endosome, and the virus can enter the cell through this process. Omicron, which emerged after SARS-CoV-2 was first identified in Wuhan, mutated and infected cells through this same route.

How the Virus Copies Itself

Once the positive-sense RNA of SARS-CoV-2 reaches the host cell’s cytoplasm, it acts directly as messenger RNA and begins producing proteins. Using the host cell’s ribosomes, the viral RNA first produces the virus’s non-structural proteins. There are sixteen of them in total, and at the start of infection they are the virus’s main weapons. The non-structural proteins quickly begin to disrupt the host cell’s biological processes and redirect them toward viral replication. Early in infection, they build special structures inside the host cell that suppress the body’s early immune defenses and help speed up viral replication.

SARS-CoV-2 replicates differently from many other viruses. Its RNA is copied in the host cell’s cytoplasm. This virus never enters the cell’s nucleus and has no way to integrate into our DNA. As soon as SARS-CoV-2 infects a cell, the newly made proteins first build special structures inside it, whose membranes shield the viral RNA and its replication from the body’s immune system.

As soon as SARS-CoV-2 enters the cytoplasm of a human cell, it begins multiplying at extraordinary speed. Replication starts when an enzyme called RNA-dependent RNA polymerase makes a reverse (antisense) copy of the RNA. Using this as a template, forward (positive sense) copies of RNA, like those found in new viruses, are then made. Some of these RNAs are used again to make proteins, while others become the genomes of new viruses.

As COVID infection and viral replication progress, host cells become virtual virus factories. Their normal functions are gradually suppressed. The infected cells’ energy, amino acids, and ribosomes are all devoted to making new viruses. These cells eventually die, but not before producing large numbers of new viruses. The newly made viral particles leave the infected cells and spread the infection to nearby cells.

The Body’s Defense: War and Damage

A COVID-19 infection puts our body in a double bind. When infection begins, the body’s innate immune system (the early defense system) can recognize the virus’s proteins and RNA and produce cytokines, including interferons, to fight the virus. If the immune system recognizes the virus early and clears it quickly, a person has a chance of surviving a serious infection. The vaccines we receive are also intended for this purpose. But SARS-CoV-2 can suppress the body’s early defense system.

Once it begins infecting respiratory cells, the virus can produce many copies at once. COVID’s serious effects begin to appear when these newly made copies start attacking nearby cells. The infection becomes more complex, and the body’s adaptive immune system activates and joins the fight against the virus.

As the adaptive immune system begins fighting COVID in this way, serious effects start to appear in some people. In some, cytokine imbalance, blood vessel damage, and blood clotting set in, which can lead to acute respiratory syndrome, organ failure, and other serious effects. One way to understand it: becoming critically ill with COVID is the combined result of the COVID-19 virus and of the immune system fighting it.

Becoming critically ill with COVID is the combined result of the COVID-19 virus and of the immune system fighting it.

If our adaptive immune system does its job, COVID’s viral load gradually declines. After a COVID infection ends, remnants of SARS-CoV-2 do not persist in the body for long, and the virus cannot hide in the body’s cells or DNA. In almost everyone who has been infected and recovered, the virus’s RNA is gone from the body 14 to 21 days after infection.

This is the central question that puzzles science: once the virus has vanished from the body, or the PCR test comes back negative for COVID-19, why doesn’t the body signal that the war is over?

Long COVID: Why Do Problems Persist After Recovery?

SARS-CoV-2 has unique abilities that may cause many types of changes in the body. Problems that can appear later, even after COVID is over, because of changes that occurred during active infection are called long COVID, or in medical language, post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2.

The symptoms of long COVID are unusual and vary from person to person. Some feel extreme fatigue, while others experience brain fog: a clouded mind, loss of concentration, and difficulty thinking. After active SARS-CoV-2 infection ends, fragments of viral RNA have been found lingering in some cells outside the respiratory system (for example, in the gut, brain, or other tissues). These fragments can hide in small amounts for some time and continue to cause inflammation. Likewise, fragments of dead virus may remain in the body, and our immune system may keep attacking them as if they were live virus. This is also one reason people continue to sweat or feel persistent fatigue long after COVID is over.

Some people have also developed myocarditis, a serious inflammation of the heart muscle. Severe COVID infection also affects blood vessels. Microclots form in the vessels, blocking oxygen from reaching various organs. This is why some people have trouble breathing and feel fatigued for a long time. Damage to lung or heart tissue during the fight takes a long time to heal, and in some cases the immune system may go astray and attack the body’s own healthy cells (an autoimmune response).

The Rutgers Study: The Theory of ‘Immunity Theft’

There is another possibility. When the body’s entire defense system is focused on fighting the coronavirus, it loses its watch over other dormant viruses and bacteria that it has kept suppressed inside the body for years. As a result, just as prisoners escape when the jail guards leave, old infections, the criminals, get a chance to rise up again. The study suggests that long COVID may be caused not only by remnants of the coronavirus but also by hidden enemies reawakened by the body’s weakened immune state.

A detailed review by researchers at Rutgers New Jersey Medical School has examined this possibility: could this unbalanced immune state be the very foundation of long COVID? They conclude that some of long COVID’s serious symptoms are not caused by SARS-CoV-2 itself. In their review paper, they point out that these permanent but dormant viruses, bacteria, and other ‘dark antigens’ may have been reactivated because of immune disruption (immune hijacking) during the fight against COVID infection.

Remnants of Old Diseases Hidden in Our DNA

If we turn the pages of our human genetic makeup (DNA) and read it as the biography of our chromosomes, we find that its earliest chapters were written by viruses. It may sound surprising, but a large part of our DNA is, in fact, a ‘viral remnant.’ Much of our DNA consists of the remains of ancient infections: fragments of prehistoric retroviruses, broken viral enzymes, and scattered genetic husks. Our DNA is not a clean page; it is a ‘historical manuscript’ in which viruses have written their stories. So it would be no exaggeration to say we are half human and a little bit ‘virus.’

Some viruses and bacteria have evolved the ability to hide within DNA itself. For example, retroviruses such as HIV, which can cause AIDS, can integrate their DNA into our chromosomes, where it can remain for life and be passed on to future generations. The remnants of ancient retroviruses that infected our bodies have made a permanent home in our DNA as transposons, or jumping genes.

Our DNA is not a clean page; it is a ‘historical manuscript’ in which viruses have written their stories.

Some bacteria or viruses can enter the cell’s nucleus and use its DNA-copying machinery but cannot integrate into the DNA. Some viruses associated with respiratory diseases have this ability. Some viruses (EBV, CMV) and some bacteria (TB), though unable to do either, suppress their own protein production to evade the immune system’s surveillance and have developed the ability to hide in various cells and persist in our bodies for life.

As I said at the start of this article, the virus that causes COVID-19 has no such ability, but its infection can trigger many changes in the body. First, even before serious infection sets in, the virus can remodel chromatin in the body’s immune cells. Put simply, the virus can change how the cell’s instruction manual is read or used. Such immune remodeling may leave long-term effects on the immune system. In a sense, COVID-19 is not only a respiratory disease but also an immune disease.

Chromatin remodeling can disrupt cytokine balance, creating long-term obstacles to the development of monocytes that recognize viruses and to the development of T and B cells that fight them. Even after the remnants of SARS-CoV-2 are gone from the body, transcriptional processes (how DNA becomes RNA and protein) that were altered during the infection remain distorted. Think of it this way: the immune system has already learned the wrong lesson and cannot unlearn it.

Immunity Theft: War at the Border, Insecurity in the City

Another long-term effect of COVID-19 is the very immune system that clears the infection. During a complex, acute COVID-19 infection, a biological state of emergency takes hold inside our bodies. As soon as SARS-CoV-2 attacks, the body’s entire defense machinery, especially T cells, B cells, and natural killer (NK) cells, drops other work and concentrates on the front lines in the lungs and respiratory system. After a COVID-19 infection, the body’s immune system is weakened: its soldiers have either been killed in battle or are utterly exhausted.

This is where the body’s security system slips up badly in the fight against SARS-CoV-2. In scientific terms, this is called immune distraction. Imagine the country’s entire army is busy at the border fighting a foreign enemy (the coronavirus). At such a time, internal security in the capital and other cities weakens, and hidden enemies within get a chance to rise up. The same happens in our bodies. This study has raised the question and the suspicion that the danger of long-term effects after COVID may come not from an outside enemy but from remnants of old viruses that have slept in our own bodies for thousands of years, waking up again.

The danger may come not from an outside enemy but from remnants of old viruses that have slept in our own bodies.

When the body’s immune system unites to fight COVID-19, the process by which it keeps constant watch over the body (immune surveillance) weakens. The Rutgers study calls this ‘immunity theft’ by COVID. The period of COVID infection thus becomes a major hole in the immune system, the security apparatus that keeps constant watch over the body. Hidden enemies take advantage of this very hole, which can give rise to latent tuberculosis, retroviruses, herpes viruses, or the Epstein-Barr virus. Lymphopenia, the shortage of white blood cells seen in COVID patients, widens this security vacuum even further.

About 8 percent of our DNA consists of remnants of ancient retroviruses that infected our ancestors millions of years ago and later became part of our genome. Normally, our body keeps them silent by placing an epigenetic lock on them.

But the immunity theft caused by COVID-19 can break those locks. As a result, these ancient viruses or transposons become active and start producing their own proteins. In this state, the body’s immune system treats even proteins made from its own DNA as foreign and begins to attack them. The study points to a strong possibility that some of the autoimmune problems seen in long COVID, in which the body attacks its own healthy organs, may be caused by these hidden enemies reawakening.

Hidden Enemies: Tuberculosis and Other Viruses

Retroviruses can integrate into our DNA and be passed down through the generations, but many other hidden enemies can also lie dormant in the body, waiting for a chance to become active again. Among these, the reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV) has made the symptoms of long COVID even more mysterious.

About 95 percent of adults worldwide have been infected with EBV. Likewise, CMV has infected 85 percent of the world’s people. Our immune system recognizes this childhood infection and clears it easily. Even so, small amounts of the virus may persist and remain hidden in the body for life. Normally, in almost everyone infected, our immune system’s surveillance keeps these small amounts of lingering virus in check.

When the body’s immune system digs in to fight COVID-19, immune surveillance weakens elsewhere in the body, and these old, opportunistic viruses lying dormant get a chance to rise up. As the Rutgers study shows, when COVID-19 erodes the function of the immune system’s soldiers—the T, B, and natural killer cells—EBV can be reawakened. This may be why the rate of patients arriving at hospitals with reactivated EBV has been rising by ten percent every year since the COVID pandemic.

The brain fog, extreme fatigue, and neurological weakness that long COVID patients experience closely resemble the symptoms of active EBV. Likewise, when CMV becomes active, it causes inflammation in blood vessels and accelerates the entire immune system’s aging (immune aging). This is why, even at 30 or 40, the body can begin to feel the fatigue and weakness of someone aged 60 or 70.

For a country like Nepal, however, the most worrying issue is the reactivation of latent tuberculosis, or latent TB. In a large part of our population, TB bacteria lie dormant within small nodules (granulomas) in the lungs. The excessive inflammation that COVID-19 brings risks breaking down the structure of these nodules that keep the bacteria confined. Just as prisoners escape when the jail walls crumble, these bacteria begin to spread through the lungs.

This is where the problem becomes even more complicated. The symptoms of active TB and long COVID (a persistent cough, evening fevers, weight loss, and extreme fatigue) are very similar. As a result, patients and doctors may mistake them for the ordinary after-effects of COVID, or simply long COVID. This study makes us seriously consider that if health problems persist for a long time after COVID, they may not be just the virus’s effect but tuberculosis that COVID has awakened. Therefore, when managing long COVID patients in Nepal, TB testing should be a mandatory priority.

For a country like Nepal, the most worrying issue is the reactivation of latent tuberculosis.

Another Danger: Immune Amnesia After COVID

Another far-reaching and frightening effect of COVID-19 infection is immune amnesia, or immune forgetting. Just as old files are lost when a computer is formatted, a severe COVID-19 infection can damage our immune system’s memory bank.

As mentioned in the Rutgers review, there are signs that COVID, like measles, can wipe out the body’s store of memory B cells and antibodies. This means that after COVID-19, our bodies may forget the vaccines we received in childhood or the diseases we fought and beat in the past. As a result, even after recovering from COVID, people remain at risk of easily falling prey to pneumonia, the flu, or other common infections.

In the end, we must understand that COVID-19 turns out to be more than just a viral infection. A COVID-19 infection can also trigger an imbalance in the body’s immune system and awaken enemies that have hidden in our genes and bodies since ancient times. In treating long COVID, which appears sometime after COVID, there now seems to be a need for diagnosis and treatment that accounts not only for the coronavirus but also for the old infections it has reawakened. COVID-19 has taught us a new lesson: the virus may be gone, but we still have much to prepare before we can fight the biological shadow it leaves behind.

(This article focuses on the question raised by this research published from Rutgers.)

  • Why Does the Body Treat a New Kidney as an Enemy?
  • Dark antigens and Transposons
